slides.heading: Welcome aboard

lines: Rules of the Road: the module that needs 90%
15 lessons, Rules 1 through 37 and the annexes
A short lesson check after every lesson

slides.video: Instructor on a charter boat’s flybridge at the dock, early morning.

slides.heading: Picture this

lines: 5:30 a.m.: you leave the dock in Tampa Bay
You run out past Egmont Key into the Gulf
Somewhere on that run, the rules changed

slides.video: Drone shot: a charter boat running down Tampa Bay at dawn and out past Egmont Key.
slides.script: Let’s start with a picture. [+] It’s five-thirty in the morning, and you’re leaving the dock in Tampa Bay with four anglers aboard. [+] You run down the bay, out past Egmont Key, and into the open Gulf to fish a ledge. [+] Here’s my question. Somewhere on that run, the rules you were following changed. Did you notice? [pause] Most captains never do, because the differences are small. But they’re real, and the exam loves them. In the bay, you were under the Inland rules. Out in the Gulf, you were under the International rules. So let’s find that line.

slides.heading: Two sets of rules

head: International (COLREGS)
Inland
rows: High seas and connected waters, seaward of the demarcation lines
U.S. inland waters, shoreward of the demarcation lines
All vessels on U.S. inland waters, and U.S. vessels on Canadian Great Lakes waters

slides.video: Chart close-up: a dashed magenta COLREGS demarcation line across a Florida inlet.
slides.script: There are two rule books, and they’re mostly identical. [+] The International rules, usually called the COLREGS, govern the high seas and the waters connected to them. [+] They come from a 1972 treaty, while the Inland rules are American law, covering our harbors, bays, rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway. [+] Each set applies to every vessel on its waters, whatever flag she flies. [pause] So where’s the line? It’s called the COLREGS demarcation line, and it’s printed on your chart as a dashed magenta line, usually stretched across the mouth of a harbor or inlet. In Florida, you cross it every time you head out an inlet. Here’s some homework: find it on your local chart this week. It makes all of this real.

slides.heading: Rule 1: what can sit alongside the rules

items: Special local rules for harbors, rivers and lakes, conforming as closely as possible
Extra station or signal lights for warships, convoys and fishing fleets
Traffic separation schemes adopted by IMO
Vessels of special construction comply as closely as possible

slides.video: Navy ship at a Florida port at dusk, showing unusual extra lights.
slides.script: Rule one also tells you what can sit alongside these rules, and there are four things to know. [+] First, local authorities can make special rules for a particular harbor, river or lake. But those rules must conform as closely as possible to the Navigation Rules. They can add to them, not throw them out. [+] Second, governments can allow extra lights, shapes or whistle signals for warships, convoys, or fishing fleets working together. So if you see an odd light on a Navy ship, that’s why. [+] Third, traffic separation schemes, the highway lanes for big ships, are adopted internationally. We’ll cover them in lesson four. [+] And fourth, a vessel of unusual construction that can’t place her lights exactly as required may use the closest alternative her government approves. Inland, that’s called a certificate of alternative compliance.

slides.heading: Rule 2: the rule above all rules

items: No rule excuses neglect of ordinary seamanship
Have due regard to all dangers and special circumstances
Depart from the rules when needed to avoid immediate danger
The rules say who keeps clear, not who has a “right of way”

slides.video: A tug pushing a barge in a channel while a small boat holds course toward it, then turns away.
slides.script: Now, Rule two. If you remember only one rule from this whole course, make it this one. [+] Rule two says nothing in the rules excuses you from the consequences of neglecting ordinary seamanship. In plain English: the rule book is not a shield. [+] You must pay attention to every danger and every special circumstance, including what the other boat can and can’t do. [+] And sometimes, to avoid immediate danger, you have to depart from the rules. That isn’t just allowed, it’s expected. [pause] Here’s how I think about it. Picture yourself as the stand-on boat, holding your course, while a tug pushing a barge clearly isn’t turning. If you hold your course right into that barge, you followed the rules, and you’ll still be found at fault. [+] Notice too that the rules almost never say right of way. They say who keeps out of the way, and who stands on. That’s a mindset, not a privilege.

slides.heading: The annexes

head: Annex
Covers
rows: Positioning and technical details of lights and shapes
Extra signals for fishing vessels fishing close together
Technical details of sound signal appliances
Inland only: pilot rules, such as law enforcement lights and special anchorage areas

slides.video: Montage: a masthead light being mounted, a ship’s whistle, a red hand flare, a law enforcement boat’s blue light.
slides.script: The rules end with annexes, and yes, the exam asks about them. Let me give you a one-line handle on each. [+] Annex one is the engineering annex: exactly where lights go, how far apart, how bright. [+] Annex two covers extra signals for fishing boats working close together, like trawlers in a fleet. [+] Annex three is the technical spec for whistles, bells and gongs. [+] Annex four is the big one for you: distress signals. We’ll spend real time on those in lesson fourteen. [+] And the Inland rules add Annex five, the pilot rules, which cover things like the blue lights on law enforcement boats and special anchorage areas.

And the Inland rules add Annex five, the pilot rules, which cover things like the blue lights on law enforcement boats and special anchorage areas.

slides.heading: Four exam habits

items: Find INLAND, INTERNATIONAL or BOTH first
Watch vessel lengths: 7, 12, 20, 50 and 100 m
“In sight of one another” or restricted visibility?
Choose the answer that matches the rule’s wording

slides.video: Close-up of a pencil circling the word INLAND on a printed exam question.
slides.script: Before we move on, here are four habits that will save you points on every rules question. [+] First, find the word Inland, International or Both at the start of the question, and answer for that rule book. Circle it if you’re on paper. [+] Second, watch vessel lengths. Seven, twelve, twenty, fifty and one hundred meters are the magic numbers, and rules change at each one. [+] Third, ask yourself: are these boats in sight of each other, or are we in fog? Different rules apply, and you’ll see why in lesson eight. [+] And fourth, when two answers both sound reasonable, pick the one that matches the rule’s actual wording. The exam is written straight from the rule book, not from what people do at the dock. [pause] That’s lesson one. Next, we’ll nail down the definitions, the vocabulary every other rule depends on.

slides.heading: Why definitions matter

lines: Every rule depends on Rule 3’s definitions
Many exam questions are definitions in disguise
Get these right and later lessons get easier

slides.video: Instructor at the helm, Rule 3 text visible in the handbook on the console.
slides.script: Today’s lesson might sound dry, definitions, but stay with me, because this is where a lot of easy points live. [+] Every rule we’ll study depends on the words defined in Rule three. Is that boat sailing or power-driven? Is she underway? Is she engaged in fishing? [+] A huge number of exam questions are really definition questions in disguise. [+] Get these words right, and every later lesson gets easier. So let’s go through them the way a captain would, with real examples.
slides.spoken: Today’s lesson might sound dry, definitions, but stay with me, because this is where a lot of easy points live. Every rule we’ll study depends on the words defined in Rule three. Is that boat sailing or power-driven? Is she underway? Is she engaged in fishing? A huge number of exam questions are really definition questions in disguise. Get these words right, and every later lesson gets easier. So let’s go through them the way a captain would, with real examples.

slides.heading: Kinds of vessels

items: Vessel: every watercraft, including non-displacement craft, WIG craft and seaplanes
Power-driven vessel: propelled by machinery
Sailing vessel: under sail, with any engine not being used
Seaplane: an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water

slides.video: A sailboat motoring out a Florida pass with sails up and engine running.
slides.script: First, what counts as a vessel? [+] Pretty much anything that floats and can carry people or things across the water: boats, ships, barges, hovercraft, even seaplanes and wing-in-ground craft. [+] A power-driven vessel is anything propelled by machinery. Simple. [+] A sailing vessel is under sail, with one important catch: any engine she has must not be in use. [pause] So here’s a classic exam question. A sailboat is heading out the pass with every sail up, and her engine is running to help her along. What is she? [pause] She’s a power-driven vessel. The moment that engine turns the prop, the rules treat her like any other powerboat. [+] And a seaplane is simply an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water.

A sailboat is heading out the pass with every sail up, and her engine is running to help her along. What is she? She’s a power-driven vessel. The moment that engine turns the prop, the rules treat her like any other powerboat. And a seaplane is simply an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water.

slides.heading: “Engaged in fishing”

items: Nets, lines, trawls or other gear that restrict maneuverability
Does NOT include trolling lines
A charter boat trolling or drifting with rods out is power-driven
A trawler heading home with gear stowed is power-driven

slides.video: Split screen: a charter boat trolling four lines beside a shrimp boat working its nets.
slides.script: Now one that matters to you as a charter captain: engaged in fishing. [+] Under the rules, it means fishing with nets, lines, trawls or other gear that restricts your ability to maneuver. [+] And here’s the key: it does not include trolling lines. [pause] So picture your morning. You’ve got four lines out, trolling for kingfish along the beach. Are you engaged in fishing? [+] No. Legally you’re just a power-driven vessel. You get no special privileges, and you keep clear of sailboats like any other powerboat. [+] Meanwhile, the shrimp boat working her nets nearby is engaged in fishing. But when that same shrimper stows her nets and heads home, she’s an ordinary power-driven vessel too. It’s about what the gear is doing, not what kind of boat it is.

slides.heading: Broken or busy?

head: Not under command
Restricted in ability to maneuver
rows: Dredging; buoy, cable or pipeline work; surveying; diving; a tow that limits her course

slides.video: A disabled sportfisher drifting with no power, then a dredge working in a channel.
slides.script: These two get mixed up all the time, so let’s separate them. [+] Not under command is about cause: some exceptional circumstance, like a failed engine or a jammed rudder, means the vessel can’t maneuver as the rules require. [+] So the word to remember is broken. [+] Restricted in her ability to maneuver is about work: the job she’s doing keeps her from getting out of the way. Dredging, laying cable, servicing a buoy, diving operations, surveying, or a tow that pins her to her course. [pause] Here’s my trick. Ask yourself: is she broken, or is she busy? Broken means not under command. Busy means restricted.

Broken means not under command. Busy means restricted.

slides.heading: Underway, or making way?

items: Constrained by draft: International only; a big ship limited by depth and channel width
Underway: not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground
Making way: moving through the water under her own power
Drifting over a wreck: underway, but not making way

slides.video: A charter boat drifting with engines off over a wreck, anglers bottom fishing.
slides.script: Next, a category that only exists offshore. [+] Constrained by her draft is International only. It’s a big ship whose draft, compared with the depth and width of the water, means she really can’t deviate from her course. You won’t find it in the Inland rules at all. [+] Now, underway. A vessel is underway if she’s not at anchor, not made fast to the shore, and not aground. [+] Making way means actually moving through the water under her own power. [pause] So imagine you shut down to drift over a wreck. You’re not anchored, not tied up, and not aground. [+] You’re underway, but not making way. As you’ll see later, both your lights and your fog signals depend on that difference.

So imagine you shut down to drift over a wreck. You’re not anchored, not tied up, and not aground. You’re underway, but not making way. As you’ll see later, both your lights and your fog signals depend on that difference.

slides.heading: In sight, and visibility

items: Length and breadth: length overall and greatest breadth
In sight of one another: seen with the eyes, not electronics
Restricted visibility: fog, mist, snow, heavy rain, sandstorms; not darkness
A radar or AIS contact in fog is NOT “in sight”

slides.video: A radar screen showing a target in fog, then the same boat emerging from the fog.
slides.script: A few more precise phrases. [+] Length and breadth mean length overall and greatest breadth. Nothing fancy. [+] In sight of one another means one vessel can actually be seen visually from the other. Eyes, not electronics. [+] Restricted visibility means visibility reduced by fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rain, sandstorms or anything similar. Notice what’s not on that list: darkness. A clear night is not restricted visibility. [+] And here’s the one that catches people. If you see a target on your radar or AIS in thick fog, you are not in sight of that vessel. That single fact decides which steering rules apply, and we’ll lean on it heavily in lesson eight.

slides.heading: Inland-only definitions

items: Inland waters: navigable U.S. waters shoreward of the demarcation lines
Great Lakes: including connecting and tributary waters
Western Rivers: the Mississippi system, with the Atchafalaya and Red Rivers
When a question names these waters, expect a special rule

slides.video: Map animation highlighting U.S. inland waters, the Great Lakes and the Mississippi river system.
slides.script: Finally, the Inland rules add a few definitions of their own. [+] Inland waters are the navigable waters of the United States shoreward of the demarcation lines. [+] The Great Lakes include their connecting and tributary waters. [+] The Western Rivers are the Mississippi River system, including the Atchafalaya and the Red River. [+] When a question mentions any of these places, expect a special rule. You may never run a charter on the Mississippi, but the exam will still ask about it. [pause] That’s our vocabulary. Next, we’ll put it to work with the duties every vessel has in any visibility: lookout, safe speed, and judging the risk of collision.

lessons.title: Lookout, safe speed and risk of collision

slides.heading: The lookout

items: Rules 4 to 10 apply in any condition of visibility
Lookout by sight and hearing, at all times
Use every available means: radar, AIS, radio
Goal: a full appraisal of the situation and the risk

slides.video: A busy charter cockpit: fish on, lines tangled, and the captain glancing forward.
slides.script: Let’s start with the duty that shows up in nearly every collision report: the lookout. [+] Rules four through ten apply in any visibility, clear or foggy, day or night. [+] Rule five says every vessel shall at all times keep a proper lookout, by sight and by hearing. [+] And by all available means. If you have radar, AIS and a VHF, they’re part of your lookout. [+] The goal is a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision. [pause] Now be honest with yourself. On a busy charter, with a fish on, a tangled line, and a customer asking a question, who’s keeping the lookout? If the answer is nobody, that’s exactly the gap where accidents happen.

slides.heading: Rule 6: safe speed

items: Visibility
Traffic density, including fishing boats
Your stopping distance and turning ability
Background lights at night
Wind, sea, current and nearby hazards
Draft compared to available depth

slides.video: Night view from a helm: a boat’s running lights almost lost against the condo lights of Clearwater Beach.
slides.script: Rule six is safe speed, and the first thing to know is that there’s no number in it. Safe speed means you can take proper action to avoid a collision, and stop within a distance that fits the conditions. So you weigh the factors. [+] Visibility, obviously. [+] Traffic density, including clusters of fishing boats. [+] Your own boat’s maneuverability: how fast she stops, how tightly she turns. [+] At night, background lights. Try picking out a running light against the condo lights of Clearwater Beach. [+] The state of the wind, sea and current, and nearby hazards. [+] And your draft compared to the depth of the water. [pause] Twenty knots might be perfectly safe in the open Gulf at noon, and reckless in the Intracoastal at dusk.

slides.heading: Safe speed with radar

items: Radar’s characteristics, efficiency and limitations
Limits of the range scale in use
Sea state, rain and interference hiding targets
Small boats and floating objects may go undetected
How many vessels radar shows, and how they move
A better measure of visibility, using radar ranges

slides.video: Radar display with sea clutter turned up, hiding a small boat target, then clutter reduced.
slides.script: If you have radar, Rule six adds six more factors, and they boil down to one idea: radar is a tool with limits. [+] Know your radar’s characteristics, efficiency and limitations. [+] Know what the range scale you’ve selected can and can’t show you. [+] Sea state, rain and interference can hide targets in clutter. [+] Small boats, logs and other floating objects may not show up until they’re close. [+] Radar tells you how many vessels are around and how they’re moving. [+] And it can give you a more exact measure of visibility, by showing how far away that boat is that you can just barely see. [pause] The exam trap is assuming radar lets you go faster. It doesn’t. It just gives you better information for judging what’s safe.

slides.heading: Rule 7: is there a risk of collision?
slides.video: Bow-mounted camera: another boat holding the same spot against the windshield frame as it grows larger.
slides.script: Rule seven is about one question: is there a risk of collision? And it starts with a powerful sentence: if there’s any doubt, the risk shall be deemed to exist. Doubt means yes. [pause] So how do you judge it? Look at the diagram. You’re the boat at the bottom, heading up the page, and another boat is crossing from your right. Each dashed line is a bearing taken a minute or so apart. See how the lines stay parallel? The bearing isn’t changing, while the distance shrinks. That’s the classic sign of a collision course. [pause] You can do this with your eyes, too. Line the other boat up with a stanchion or a corner of your windshield. If it stays in that spot while it gets bigger, you’re on a collision course. One warning: with a very large ship, a tow, or anything very close, risk can exist even when the bearing is changing.

slides.heading: Captain’s example: one glance isn’t enough

lines: Fog off Port Everglades
One radar glance: a target 3 miles ahead
Plot it for a few minutes before you decide

slides.video: Fog over the Port Everglades entrance; radar screen with a target being marked every minute.
slides.script: Rule seven also covers radar, so here’s a scenario. [+] Imagine you’re heading out of Port Everglades on a rare foggy morning. [+] You glance at the radar and see a target about three miles ahead. One look tells you almost nothing: where it’s going, how fast, whether it’ll pass clear. [+] Rule seven says radar must be used properly, with long-range scanning for early warning, and radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation. Mark the target, watch it for a few minutes, and see how it moves. [pause] And the rule adds a sentence worth memorizing: assumptions shall not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information. One glance is scanty. A plot is information.

slides.heading: Rule 8: how to act

items: Positive, made in ample time, with good seamanship
Large enough to be obvious by eye or radar
Avoid a series of small alterations
A course change alone may be best, if early, substantial and safe

slides.video: Overhead drone: one boat makes a bold 40-degree turn while another weaves with small course changes.
slides.script: Once you’ve decided there’s a risk, Rule eight tells you how to act. [+] Your action should be positive, made in ample time, and with good seamanship. [+] It should be big enough to be obvious, whether the other captain is watching with his eyes or on radar. A five degree nudge is invisible. A forty degree turn tells a story. [+] Which is why the rule says to avoid a series of small alterations. [+] And if you have sea room, a course change alone is often your best move, as long as it’s early, substantial, and doesn’t just set you up for another close call with someone else. [pause] Think of it like driving: signal clearly, commit, and don’t weave.

slides.heading: Passing clear, and “not to impede”

items: Pass at a safe distance; keep checking until finally past and clear
Slow, stop or back down to buy time
“Not to impede”: act early to leave plenty of room
That duty continues even when risk of collision develops

slides.video: A small boat slowing and turning early to give a ship in the channel plenty of room.
slides.script: Two more parts of Rule eight. [+] Your action must get you past at a safe distance, and you keep checking that it’s working until the other vessel is finally past and clear. [+] If you need more time to figure things out, slow down, stop, or back down. Slowing down is always on the menu, and it buys you time. [+] Rule eight also defines a phrase you’ll meet again and again: not to impede. A vessel required not to impede another must act early, leaving plenty of room. [+] And that duty doesn’t disappear just because the boats get close and a risk of collision develops. [pause] That’s lesson three. Next time, we’ll head into narrow channels and the big-ship highways called traffic separation schemes, where small boats like ours have special duties.

lessons.title: Narrow channels and traffic separation schemes

slides.heading: Rule 9: keep to starboard, don’t impede
slides.script: Rule nine covers narrow channels and fairways, like the dredged ship channels into Tampa Bay, Port Everglades or Jacksonville. A vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway shall keep as near to the outer limit of the channel on her starboard side as is safe and practicable. So vessels meeting in a channel each stay right and pass port to port. A vessel of less than twenty meters, or any sailing vessel, shall not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel. For most six-pack charter boats, that means you stay out of the way of the ships.

slides.heading: Fishing, crossing and anchoring in channels

items: Fishing vessels shall not impede any vessel navigating within the channel
Don’t cross if it impedes a vessel that must stay in the channel
That vessel may sound the danger signal if in doubt
Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel

slides.script: Rule nine continues. A vessel engaged in fishing shall not impede the passage of any other vessel navigating within a narrow channel or fairway. A vessel shall not cross a narrow channel if the crossing impedes a vessel that can safely navigate only within it, and that vessel may sound the danger signal of at least five short blasts if she is in doubt about the crossing vessel’s intentions. And every vessel shall, if circumstances admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel. Anchoring a charter boat to fish the edge of a ship channel is exactly what this rule discourages.

slides.heading: Overtaking and bends

items: Overtaking that needs the other vessel’s help requires signals and agreement
The vessel being overtaken acts to permit safe passing
Rule 13 still makes the overtaking vessel keep clear
Blind bend: one prolonged blast, answered by one prolonged blast

slides.script: When one vessel can overtake another in a narrow channel only if the vessel being overtaken takes action to permit safe passing, the overtaking vessel signals her intention with the whistle signals of Rule thirty-four. The vessel being overtaken signals her agreement and takes steps to permit the pass, or sounds the danger signal if in doubt. Rule thirteen still applies, so the overtaking vessel remains responsible for keeping clear. A vessel nearing a bend or an area where other vessels may be hidden by an obstruction shall navigate with particular alertness and caution, and sound one prolonged blast. Any vessel around the bend that hears it answers with one prolonged blast.

slides.heading: Inland Rule 9: downbound vessels

items: Great Lakes, Western Rivers and specified waters only
A downbound power-driven vessel with a following current has right of way
She proposes the manner and place of passage
She initiates the maneuvering signals
The upbound vessel holds as necessary to permit safe passing

slides.script: The Inland version of Rule nine adds a special rule for the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers and other waters the Coast Guard specifies. In narrow channels there, a power-driven vessel proceeding downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel. She proposes the manner and place of passage and initiates the maneuvering signals. The vessel proceeding upbound against the current holds as necessary to permit safe passing. The logic is simple: a vessel going downstream with the current has less control and can’t easily stop.

slides.heading: Rule 10: traffic separation schemes
slides.script: Rule ten covers traffic separation schemes, which work like a divided highway at sea, with a lane for each direction and a separation zone between them. A vessel using a scheme shall proceed in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow, keep clear of the separation line or zone, and normally join or leave at the end of a lane. If she joins or leaves from the side, she does so at as small an angle to the general direction of traffic as practicable. A vessel shall, as far as practicable, avoid crossing traffic lanes, but if obliged to cross, she does so on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow.

If she joins or leaves from the side, she does so at as small an angle to the general direction of traffic as practicable. A vessel shall, as far as practicable, avoid crossing traffic lanes, but if obliged to cross, she does so on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow.

slides.heading: Rule 10: who uses what

items: Through traffic stays out of inshore traffic zones
Under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels may use inshore zones
Under 20 m and sailing vessels don’t impede power vessels in a lane
Fishing vessels don’t impede vessels following a lane
Avoid anchoring in a scheme or near its ends
Not using the scheme? Avoid it by a wide margin

slides.script: Through traffic shall not use an inshore traffic zone when it can safely use the adjacent lane. However, vessels of less than twenty meters, sailing vessels and vessels engaged in fishing may use the inshore traffic zone, and any vessel may use it when going to or from a place within it, or to avoid immediate danger. Vessels of less than twenty meters and sailing vessels shall not impede the safe passage of a power-driven vessel following a traffic lane, and a fishing vessel shall not impede any vessel following a lane. Vessels should avoid anchoring within a scheme or near its terminations, and a vessel not using a scheme should avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable.

Vessels should avoid anchoring within a scheme or near its terminations, and a vessel not using a scheme should avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable.

slides.heading: Rule 11: vessels in sight

items: Rules 11 to 18 apply only to vessels in sight of one another
In restricted visibility and not in sight, Rule 19 applies instead
Radar contact alone doesn’t make vessels “in sight”

slides.script: Lesson five starts the second section of the steering rules. Rule eleven says that Rules twelve through eighteen apply only to vessels in sight of one another. That phrase is precise. Remember from the definitions that vessels are in sight only when one can be observed visually from the other. If you’re in fog and see a vessel only on radar, you are not in sight, and none of the stand-on or give-way rules apply. Instead, Rule nineteen, conduct in restricted visibility, governs both vessels. We’ll cover Rule nineteen in lesson eight.

slides.heading: Rule 12: two sailing vessels

items: Wind on different sides: the boat with wind on her port side keeps clear
Wind on the same side: the windward boat keeps clear
Port-tack boat can’t tell the other’s tack: she keeps clear
Windward side: opposite the side the mainsail is carried

slides.script: Rule twelve decides between two sailing vessels approaching each other. When each has the wind on a different side, the vessel with the wind on her port side keeps out of the way. When both have the wind on the same side, the vessel to windward keeps out of the way of the vessel to leeward. If a vessel with the wind on her port side sees a vessel to windward and can’t determine whether that vessel has the wind on her port or starboard side, she keeps out of the way. For this rule, the windward side is the side opposite to the one on which the mainsail is carried. On a square-rigged vessel, it’s the side opposite the largest fore-and-aft sail.

When both have the wind on the same side, the vessel to windward keeps out of the way of the vessel to leeward. If a vessel with the wind on her port side sees a vessel to windward and can’t determine whether that vessel has the wind on her port or starboard side, she keeps out of the way. For this rule, the windward side is the side opposite to the one on which the mainsail is carried. On a square-rigged vessel, it’s the side opposite the largest fore-and-aft sail.

slides.heading: Rule 13: overtaking
slides.script: Rule thirteen covers overtaking, and it overrides everything in Rules four through eighteen. Any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken. A vessel is overtaking when she comes up with another from a direction more than twenty-two and a half degrees abaft her beam. That’s the shaded zone in this picture. At night, the overtaking vessel would be able to see only the sternlight of the vessel ahead, and neither of her sidelights. Because overtaking overrides Rule eighteen, a sailboat overtaking a power-driven vessel must keep clear, and so must a fishing vessel overtaking anyone.

At night, the overtaking vessel would be able to see only the sternlight of the vessel ahead, and neither of her sidelights. Because overtaking overrides Rule eighteen, a sailboat overtaking a power-driven vessel must keep clear, and so must a fishing vessel overtaking anyone.

slides.heading: Overtaking: the fine print

items: In doubt? Assume you’re overtaking
A later change of bearing doesn’t make it a crossing
Keep clear until finally past and clear
Overtaking overrides Rules 4 to 18

slides.script: When a vessel is in any doubt whether she is overtaking another, she shall assume that she is and act accordingly. Any later alteration of the bearing between the two vessels does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel, or relieve her of the duty of keeping clear. So if you start overtaking a boat from astern, and she alters course so that you end up on her beam, you are still the overtaking vessel. You remain the give-way vessel until you are finally past and clear. Notice the words finally past and clear. Getting your bow just ahead isn’t enough.

You remain the give-way vessel until you are finally past and clear. Notice the words finally past and clear. Getting your bow just ahead isn’t enough.

slides.heading: Overtaking meets the pecking order

items: Power overtaking sail: power keeps clear
Sail overtaking power: sail keeps clear
Fishing vessel overtaking anyone: the fishing vessel keeps clear
Coming up from astern? The overtaking vessel keeps clear

slides.script: Let’s test the overtaking rule against the pecking order of Rule eighteen. A power-driven vessel overtaking a sailboat keeps clear. That’s Rule thirteen and Rule eighteen agreeing. A sailboat overtaking a power-driven vessel also keeps clear, because overtaking overrides the pecking order. A fishing vessel overtaking a pleasure boat keeps clear for the same reason. On the exam, when a question describes one vessel coming up on another from astern, the overtaking vessel is the one that keeps clear, whatever kind of vessel she is.

On the exam, when a question describes one vessel coming up on another from astern, the overtaking vessel is the one that keeps clear, whatever kind of vessel she is.

slides.heading: Rule 14: head-on
slides.script: Rule fourteen covers two power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses so as to involve risk of collision. Each shall alter her course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other. Such a situation exists when a vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead. By night she would see the masthead lights of the other in a line or nearly in a line, or both sidelights, or both. By day, she would observe the corresponding aspect of the other vessel. When a vessel is in any doubt whether such a situation exists, she shall assume that it does and act accordingly. Neither vessel is the stand-on vessel in a head-on situation.

Each shall alter her course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other. Such a situation exists when a vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead. By night she would see the masthead lights of the other in a line or nearly in a line, or both sidelights, or both. By day, she would observe the corresponding aspect of the other vessel. When a vessel is in any doubt whether such a situation exists, she shall assume that it does and act accordingly. Neither vessel is the stand-on vessel in a head-on situation.

slides.heading: Inland: rivers

items: Great Lakes, Western Rivers and specified waters only
Meeting: a downbound power vessel with a following current has right of way
She proposes the manner of passage and initiates the signals
A power vessel crossing a river keeps clear of power vessels going up or down it

slides.script: Inland adds two special rules for rivers. On the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers and specified waters, a power-driven vessel operating downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel when they meet. She proposes the manner and place of passage and initiates the maneuvering signals, and the upbound vessel holds as necessary to permit safe passing. And on those same waters, a power-driven vessel crossing a river shall keep out of the way of a power-driven vessel ascending or descending the river.

And on those same waters, a power-driven vessel crossing a river shall keep out of the way of a power-driven vessel ascending or descending the river.

slides.heading: Rule 15: crossing
slides.script: Rule fifteen covers two power-driven vessels crossing so as to involve risk of collision. The vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way and, if circumstances admit, avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel. In this picture, the lower boat sees the other on her starboard side, so she is the give-way vessel. Her best move is usually a clear turn to starboard, passing astern of the other boat. A handy memory aid: if you can see the other vessel’s red sidelight, you are the give-way vessel. If you see her green sidelight, you are the stand-on vessel, and you hold your course and speed.

slides.heading: Rules 16 and 17: the duties

head: Stage
Stand-on vessel
rows: MAY act by her own maneuver alone
Give-way vessel alone can’t avoid collision
SHALL take the action that best aids to avoid collision

slides.script: Rule sixteen says every give-way vessel shall, so far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear. Rule seventeen describes the stand-on vessel’s duty in three stages. First, when risk of collision develops, she shall keep her course and speed. Second, once it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, she may take action to avoid collision by her maneuver alone. Sounding the danger signal at this point is good practice. Third, when she finds herself so close that collision can’t be avoided by the give-way vessel alone, she shall take such action as will best aid to avoid collision. May at stage two, shall at stage three. The exam tests that difference.

slides.heading: Rule 17: two more details

items: Crossing: a stand-on power vessel avoids turning to port for a vessel on her own port side
Stand-on action never relieves the give-way vessel
Keep course and speed means predictable, not reckless

slides.script: Two more details of Rule seventeen. A power-driven vessel that takes action in a crossing situation to avoid collision with another power-driven vessel shall, if circumstances permit, not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side. Turning to port would likely carry her right across the give-way vessel’s path, just as that vessel finally turns to starboard. And Rule seventeen does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way. Whatever the stand-on vessel does, the give-way vessel is still responsible for keeping clear.

And Rule seventeen does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way. Whatever the stand-on vessel does, the give-way vessel is still responsible for keeping clear.

slides.heading: Rule 18: the ladder
slides.script: Rule eighteen sets the responsibilities between different kinds of vessels, except where Rules nine, ten and thirteen otherwise require. A power-driven vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel. Read the ladder on screen from the bottom up. Each type of vessel generally keeps out of the way of the types above it. Power-driven vessels sit at the bottom, which is where most charter boats live.

slides.heading: Up the ladder

items: Sailing vessels keep clear of: NUC, RAM, fishing
Fishing vessels keep clear, as far as possible, of: NUC, RAM
NUC and RAM sit at the top

slides.script: Moving up the ladder, a sailing vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing. A vessel engaged in fishing when underway shall, so far as possible, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver. At the top of the ladder, vessels not under command and restricted vessels have no one listed above them, because by definition they can’t easily get out of anyone’s way.

slides.heading: Constrained by draft

items: International only
Any vessel except NUC or RAM avoids impeding a CBD vessel
The CBD vessel navigates with particular caution
“Not impeding” means acting early, not stand-on or give-way

slides.script: Under International rules, any vessel other than a vessel not under command or a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shall, if circumstances admit, avoid impeding the safe passage of a vessel constrained by her draft that is showing the signals of Rule twenty-eight. The vessel constrained by her draft shall navigate with particular caution, having full regard to her special condition. Remember from Rule eight that not impeding means acting early to leave sea room. It’s different from give-way and stand-on. And remember that constrained by draft doesn’t exist under Inland rules.

The vessel constrained by her draft shall navigate with particular caution, having full regard to her special condition. Remember from Rule eight that not impeding means acting early to leave sea room. It’s different from give-way and stand-on. And remember that constrained by draft doesn’t exist under Inland rules.

slides.heading: When the ladder doesn’t apply

items: Rule 9: small and sailing vessels don’t impede ships in a narrow channel
Rule 10: the same applies in traffic lanes
Rule 13: the overtaking vessel always keeps clear
Example: a sailboat in a ship channel must not impede a tanker

slides.script: Rule eighteen opens with an important exception: except where Rules nine, ten and thirteen otherwise require. So in a narrow channel, a sailing vessel or a vessel under twenty meters must not impede a large ship that can navigate only in the channel, even though the ship is power-driven. In a traffic separation scheme, the same applies to vessels following a lane. And a vessel overtaking always keeps clear, whatever type she is. On the exam, check whether a question mentions a narrow channel, a traffic lane or overtaking before you apply the ladder.

On the exam, check whether a question mentions a narrow channel, a traffic lane or overtaking before you apply the ladder.

slides.heading: Seaplanes and WIG craft

items: Seaplane on the water: keep well clear of all vessels
If risk of collision exists, a seaplane follows the steering rules
WIG craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface: keep clear of all vessels
WIG craft on the water: follow the rules as a power-driven vessel

slides.script: Rule eighteen also covers seaplanes and wing-in-ground craft. A seaplane on the water shall, in general, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. But where risk of collision exists, she shall comply with the steering rules. A wing-in-ground craft, when taking off, landing and in flight near the surface, shall keep well clear of all other vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. When operating on the water surface, she follows the rules as a power-driven vessel.
slides.spoken: Rule eighteen also covers seaplanes and wing-in-ground craft. A seaplane on the water shall, in general, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. But where risk of collision exists, she shall comply with the steering rules. A wing-in-ground craft, when taking off, landing and in flight near the surface, shall keep well clear of all other vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. When operating on the water surface, she follows the rules as a power-driven vessel.

slides.heading: Rule 19: when it applies

items: Vessels not in sight of one another
In or near an area of restricted visibility
No stand-on or give-way vessel
Every vessel shares the duty to avoid collision

slides.script: Rule nineteen is one of the most important and most tested rules, and it’s often misunderstood. It applies to vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility. Notice the words or near. You may be in clear weather beside a fog bank. Under Rule nineteen there is no stand-on vessel and no give-way vessel. The steering rules for vessels in sight don’t apply. Every vessel has the same duty to avoid a close-quarters situation, and every vessel must take action.

slides.heading: Speed and readiness

items: Safe speed adapted to the visibility
Power-driven vessels keep engines ready for immediate maneuver
Apply Rules 4 to 10 with the visibility in mind
Sound fog signals, keep lights on, plot radar targets

slides.script: Every vessel shall proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility. A power-driven vessel shall have her engines ready for immediate maneuver. Every vessel shall have due regard to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility when complying with Rules four through ten. In practice, that means slowing down, posting an extra lookout to listen, sounding the fog signals of Rule thirty-five, keeping your navigation lights on, and plotting every radar target.

slides.heading: Radar-only contacts
slides.script: Here’s the heart of Rule nineteen. A vessel that detects another by radar alone shall determine whether a close-quarters situation is developing or risk of collision exists. If so, she shall take avoiding action in ample time. If that action is an alteration of course, then so far as possible she shall avoid two things. First, an alteration of course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than a vessel being overtaken. That’s the left picture. Second, an alteration of course toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam. That’s the right picture. For a vessel ahead, a substantial turn to starboard is usually the safe choice.

slides.heading: Hearing a fog signal

items: Hear a fog signal apparently forward of your beam?
Or can’t avoid close quarters with a vessel forward of the beam?
Reduce to the minimum speed that keeps you on course
Take all way off if necessary
Navigate with extreme caution until the danger is over

slides.script: The second key part of Rule nineteen applies unless you’ve already determined that no risk of collision exists. Every vessel that hears, apparently forward of her beam, the fog signal of another vessel, or that cannot avoid a close-quarters situation with another vessel forward of her beam, shall reduce her speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on her course. She shall, if necessary, take all her way off, and in any event navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over. Note the word apparently. Sound travels unpredictably in fog, so you can’t fully trust the direction a signal seems to come from.

slides.heading: Handing over to the other rules

items: Once you sight each other, Rules 11 to 18 apply
Radar alone never makes you “in sight”
No assumptions on scanty radar information
Fog signals are in Rule 35, lesson 14

slides.script: Finally, remember how Rule nineteen hands over to the other rules. The moment two vessels come into sight of one another visually, the rules for vessels in sight, eleven through eighteen, take over, and a stand-on and give-way vessel exist again. Until then, both vessels share the duty. Radar contact alone never puts vessels in sight of one another, and Rule seven’s warning about scanty radar information applies with full force in fog. We’ll cover the fog signals themselves, Rule thirty-five, in lesson fourteen.

lessons.title: Lights: arcs, ranges and power-driven vessels

slides.heading: Rule 20: when lights and shapes apply

items: Lights: sunset to sunrise, in all weather
Also in restricted visibility, and whenever necessary
No other lights that could be mistaken for them or spoil the lookout
Shapes: by day
Technical details: Annex I

slides.script: Part C of the rules covers lights and shapes. Rule twenty says the light rules apply from sunset to sunrise in all weathers. During that time no other lights shall be shown, except lights that can’t be mistaken for the required lights, don’t impair their visibility or distinctive character, and don’t interfere with keeping a proper lookout. Bright deck lights that blind your own lookout break this rule. Required lights shall also be shown from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility, and may be shown at any other time when necessary. The rules for shapes apply by day. Exact positions and spacing are in Annex one.

slides.heading: Rule 21: the lights defined
slides.script: Rule twenty-one defines each light. The masthead light is a white light over the centerline, showing over an arc of two hundred twenty-five degrees, from right ahead to twenty-two and a half degrees abaft the beam on either side. Sidelights are green on starboard and red on port, each showing over one hundred twelve and a half degrees, from right ahead to twenty-two and a half degrees abaft the beam on its own side. On a vessel under twenty meters, the sidelights may be combined in one lantern on the centerline. The sternlight is white, showing over one hundred thirty-five degrees aft. The towing light is yellow, with the same arc as the sternlight. An all-round light shows over three hundred sixty degrees. A flashing light flashes a hundred twenty or more times per minute.

slides.heading: Rule 22: visibility ranges (nautical miles)
slides.script: Rule twenty-two sets the minimum range at which each light must be visible, and it depends on vessel length. On vessels fifty meters or more, the masthead light must be visible six miles, and every other light three miles. On vessels from twelve to fifty meters, the masthead light must be visible five miles, but only three miles if the vessel is under twenty meters. Sidelights, sternlight, towing light and all-round lights must be visible two miles. On vessels under twelve meters, the masthead light must be visible two miles, the sidelights one mile, and the sternlight, towing and all-round lights two miles. The exam asks these numbers often, so make yourself a flashcard.

slides.script: Rule twenty-three covers power-driven vessels underway. She shows a masthead light forward, sidelights and a sternlight. A vessel fifty meters or more must also show a second masthead light abaft of and higher than the forward one. A vessel under fifty meters may show the second masthead light but isn’t required to. The two masthead lights act like a range, telling you which way a big ship is heading and when she starts to turn. A power-driven vessel under twelve meters may instead show an all-round white light and sidelights, which is what most center consoles carry.

slides.heading: Rule 23: special cases

items: Air-cushion vessel, non-displacement mode: all-round flashing yellow
WIG craft near the surface: high-intensity all-round flashing red
Under 7 m with max speed 7 knots: all-round white, sidelights if practicable

slides.script: A few special cases. An air-cushion vessel operating in the non-displacement mode adds an all-round flashing yellow light. A wing-in-ground craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface adds a high-intensity all-round flashing red light. A power-driven vessel under seven meters whose maximum speed doesn’t exceed seven knots may show an all-round white light instead, and shall, if practicable, also show sidelights. On a power-driven vessel under twelve meters, the masthead or all-round light may be off the centerline if centerline fitting isn’t practicable, provided the sidelights are combined in one lantern near the centerline. Inland, on the Great Lakes, a power-driven vessel may show an all-round white light in place of the second masthead light and the sternlight.

slides.script: Rule twenty-four covers towing and pushing. A power-driven vessel towing astern shows two masthead lights in a vertical line. When the length of the tow, measured from the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the tow, exceeds two hundred meters, she shows three masthead lights in a vertical line. She also shows sidelights, a sternlight, and a yellow towing light in a vertical line above the sternlight. A towing vessel fifty meters or more still shows her other masthead light as well. When the tow exceeds two hundred meters, both the towing vessel and the tow show a diamond shape by day where it can best be seen.

slides.script: When a pushing vessel and a vessel pushed ahead are rigidly connected in a composite unit, they are regarded as one power-driven vessel and show the lights of Rule twenty-three. Otherwise, a power-driven vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside shows two masthead lights in a vertical line and sidelights. Under International rules, she also shows a sternlight. Under Inland rules, she shows two yellow towing lights in a vertical line instead of the sternlight. So from astern at night, a single white light suggests International rules, and two yellow lights mean an Inland pushing or alongside tow. Inland, on the Western Rivers and other specified waters, a vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside shows sidelights and two towing lights, without masthead lights.

slides.script: Now the vessels being towed. A vessel or object towed astern shows sidelights and a sternlight, plus a diamond shape by day when the tow is over two hundred meters. Under International rules, a vessel being pushed ahead shows sidelights at the forward end. Under Inland rules, she shows sidelights and a special flashing light at the forward end. The special flashing light is yellow, flashes fifty to seventy times a minute, and shows forward over an arc between one hundred eighty and two hundred twenty-five degrees. A vessel towed alongside shows a sternlight and, at the forward end, sidelights. Any number of vessels pushed or towed alongside in a group are lit as one vessel.

slides.heading: Special towing situations

items: A tow that severely restricts her course: add the RAM lights and shapes
Partly submerged objects: all-round white lights at the ends, diamond aft
Can’t light the tow? Take all possible measures to show its presence
Rescue tows needn’t show towing lights if impracticable, but illuminate the towline

slides.script: Some special cases. A towing vessel whose tow severely restricts her ability to deviate from her course shows the restricted-in-ability-to-maneuver lights and shapes in addition to her towing lights. Inconspicuous, partly submerged vessels or objects being towed, like a fuel bladder, show all-round white lights at the ends, with extra lights if very wide, and a diamond shape at the aftermost end. Where it’s impracticable to light a vessel or object being towed, all possible measures shall be taken to light it or show its presence. And a vessel not normally engaged in towing, such as a boat towing another in distress, isn’t required to show towing lights when that’s impracticable, but must indicate the relationship, for example by illuminating the towline.

slides.script: Rule twenty-five covers sailing vessels and rowing boats. A sailing vessel underway shows sidelights and a sternlight, and no masthead light. On a sailing vessel under twenty meters, those lights may be combined in one tricolor lantern at or near the top of the mast, where they’re easier to see over waves. A sailing vessel may also show two all-round lights at or near the masthead, red over green, in addition to her sidelights and sternlight. Remember: red over green, sailing machine. But those optional lights may not be shown together with the tricolor lantern.

items: Sail under 7 m: sidelights and sternlight if practicable

slides.script: A sailing vessel under seven meters shall, if practicable, show sidelights and a sternlight. If she doesn’t, she must have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, exhibited in sufficient time to prevent collision. A vessel under oars may show the sailing vessel lights, but if not, she must have that same white torch or lantern ready. By day, a vessel proceeding under sail while also propelled by machinery shall show a cone, apex downward, forward where it can best be seen. Inland, a vessel under twelve meters isn’t required to show this cone, but may.

slides.script: Rule twenty-six covers vessels engaged in fishing, whether underway or at anchor. A trawler shows two all-round lights, green over white. Green over white, trawling tonight. She also shows a masthead light abaft of and higher than the green light, though a vessel under fifty meters isn’t required to. A vessel fishing other than trawling shows red over white. In both cases, when making way through the water, she adds sidelights and a sternlight.

slides.script: By day, a vessel engaged in fishing shows two cones with their apexes together, one above the other. A vessel fishing with outlying gear extending more than one hundred fifty meters also shows a cone, apex upward, in the direction of the gear. When a fishing vessel is not engaged in fishing, she shows only the normal lights or shapes for a vessel of her length. So a shrimp boat steaming home at night with her nets stowed shows ordinary power-driven lights, and has none of the privileges of a fishing vessel.

slides.script: Annex two describes extra signals for fishing vessels fishing in close proximity. These lights are placed lower than the Rule twenty-six lights and are visible at least one mile. A trawler may show two white lights in a vertical line when shooting her nets, white over red when hauling her nets, and two red lights in a vertical line when her net is fast on an obstruction. Vessels pair trawling may direct a searchlight forward and toward the other vessel of the pair. A purse seiner hampered by her gear may show two yellow lights in a vertical line, flashing alternately. The exam usually asks you to match each signal to its meaning.

slides.script: Rule twenty-seven covers vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver. A vessel not under command shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line, and by day two balls. When making way, she adds sidelights and a sternlight. A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shows three all-round lights in a vertical line, red, white, red, and by day a ball, a diamond and a ball. When making way, she adds masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight. When at anchor, she shows her restricted lights plus her anchor lights. The special lights tell you about her condition, and the other lights tell you whether she’s moving.

slides.script: A vessel engaged in dredging or underwater operations, when restricted in her ability to maneuver, also shows where an obstruction exists. Two all-round red lights in a vertical line, or two balls by day, mark the side where the obstruction is. Two all-round green lights in a vertical line, or two diamonds by day, mark the side on which another vessel may pass. When a vessel engaged in diving operations is too small to show all these lights and shapes, she shows the red, white, red all-round lights and a rigid replica of the International Code flag A, at least one meter high, visible all around. In Florida, also remember the state’s red-and-white diver-down flag.

items: Mine clearance: three all-round green lights, or three balls

slides.script: A vessel engaged in mine clearance shows three all-round green lights, or three balls by day, one near the foremast head and one at each end of the fore yard. These signals mean it is dangerous for another vessel to approach within one thousand meters. Vessels under twelve meters, except those engaged in diving operations, aren’t required to show the not-under-command or restricted signals. And remember, these signals are not distress signals. A vessel showing them is telling you about her limits, not asking for help.

slides.script: Rule twenty-eight is International only. A vessel constrained by her draft may show, in addition to her power-driven lights, three all-round red lights in a vertical line, or by day a cylinder. Rule twenty-nine covers pilot vessels on pilotage duty. She shows white over red all-round lights at or near the masthead. White over red, pilot ahead. When underway she adds sidelights and a sternlight. At anchor she adds her anchor light or lights. When a pilot vessel isn’t on pilotage duty, she shows the normal lights for a vessel of her length.

slides.heading: Rule 30: anchored and aground

items: w
Under 50 m at anchor
w

50 m and over at anchor

Aground

slides.script: Rule thirty covers anchored and aground vessels. A vessel at anchor shows an all-round white light in the fore part, and at or near the stern a second all-round white light, lower than the forward one. A vessel under fifty meters may instead show one all-round white light where it can best be seen. A vessel one hundred meters or more must also illuminate her decks with working lights. A vessel aground shows her anchor lights plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line. By day, one ball means at anchor, and three balls in a vertical line means aground.

slides.heading: Exemptions and seaplanes

items: Under 7 m at anchor, away from channels, fairways and anchorages: no anchor light or shape required
Under 12 m aground: no aground lights or shapes required
Inland: under 20 m in a special anchorage area: no anchor light or shape
Rule 31: seaplanes show lights as close as possible to the rules

slides.script: There are some exemptions to know. A vessel under seven meters at anchor, when not in or near a narrow channel, fairway or anchorage, or where other vessels normally navigate, doesn’t need anchor lights or a shape. A vessel under twelve meters aground doesn’t need the aground lights or shapes. Inland, a vessel under twenty meters at anchor in a special anchorage area designated by the Coast Guard doesn’t need anchor lights or a shape. Finally, Rule thirty-one says that where a seaplane or wing-in-ground craft can’t show lights and shapes exactly as required, she shows lights and shapes as closely similar as possible.

slides.heading: Rules 32 and 33: blasts and equipment

head: Length
Required
rows: Some means of making an efficient sound signal

slides.script: Part D covers sound and light signals. Rule thirty-two defines a whistle as any device that can produce the prescribed blasts, a short blast as about one second, and a prolonged blast as four to six seconds. Rule thirty-three sets the equipment by length. A vessel twelve meters or more must carry a whistle. A vessel twenty meters or more must carry a whistle and a bell. A vessel one hundred meters or more must also carry a gong, whose tone can’t be confused with the bell. A vessel under twelve meters isn’t required to carry these, but if she doesn’t, she must have some other means of making an efficient sound signal.

slides.heading: International maneuvering signals

items: S
Altering course to starboard
SS
Altering course to port
SSS
Operating astern propulsion

slides.script: Under International rules, when vessels are in sight of one another, a power-driven vessel underway that is maneuvering as authorized or required by the rules shall indicate that maneuver by whistle. One short blast means I am altering my course to starboard. Two short blasts means I am altering my course to port. Three short blasts means I am operating astern propulsion. These signals describe action actually being taken, and no reply is required. A vessel may supplement them with light signals on an all-round white light. Each flash lasts about one second, flashes are about one second apart, and successive signals are at least ten seconds apart.

One short blast means I am altering my course to starboard. Two short blasts means I am altering my course to port. Three short blasts means I am operating astern propulsion. These signals describe action actually being taken, and no reply is required. A vessel may supplement them with light signals on an all-round white light. Each flash lasts about one second, flashes are about one second apart, and successive signals are at least ten seconds apart.

slides.heading: Inland maneuvering signals

head: International
Inland
rows: I am altering course to starboard
I intend to leave you on my port side
I am altering course to port
I intend to leave you on my starboard side
Meeting or crossing within half a mile
Same signal to agree, or danger signal
White or yellow, with the whistle

slides.script: Inland rules use the same blasts for a different purpose. When power-driven vessels are in sight of one another and meeting or crossing at a distance within half a mile of each other, each vessel shall indicate her intended maneuver. One short blast means I intend to leave you on my port side. Two short blasts means I intend to leave you on my starboard side. Three short blasts means I am operating astern propulsion. Upon hearing the one or two blast signal, the other vessel shall, if in agreement, sound the same whistle signal and take the steps needed to pass. If she doubts the safety of the proposal, she sounds the danger signal. Inland light signals may be white or yellow, and are synchronized with the whistle.

slides.heading: Overtaking signals

items: PPS
Intl: on your starboard side
PPSS
Intl: on your port side
PSPS
Intl: agreement

slides.script: Overtaking signals differ too. Under International rules, in a narrow channel or fairway, two prolonged blasts followed by one short means I intend to overtake you on your starboard side. Two prolonged followed by two short means I intend to overtake you on your port side. The vessel about to be overtaken signals agreement with one prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short. Under Inland rules, overtaking signals apply between power-driven vessels in sight of one another in any waters, not just channels. One short blast means I intend to overtake you on your starboard side, two short means on your port side, and the vessel being overtaken answers with the same signal if she agrees, or the danger signal if she doesn’t.

One short blast means I intend to overtake you on your starboard side, two short means on your port side, and the vessel being overtaken answers with the same signal if she agrees, or the danger signal if she doesn’t.

slides.heading: Danger, bends and berths

items: SSSSS
Danger or doubt
P
Bend; Inland, leaving a berth

slides.script: When vessels in sight are approaching each other and either fails to understand the other’s intentions, or doubts the other is taking enough action, she shall immediately sound at least five short and rapid blasts. That’s the danger or doubt signal, and it may be supplemented by at least five short and rapid flashes. A vessel nearing a bend or area where other vessels may be hidden sounds one prolonged blast, and any vessel around the bend that hears it answers with one prolonged blast. Inland, a power-driven vessel leaving a dock or berth sounds one prolonged blast. And if a vessel has whistles more than one hundred meters apart, only one whistle is used for maneuvering signals.

A vessel nearing a bend or area where other vessels may be hidden sounds one prolonged blast, and any vessel around the bend that hears it answers with one prolonged blast. slides.heading: Radio agreements

items: Inland: agreement by radiotelephone means whistle signals aren’t required
No agreement? Exchange whistle signals, and they prevail
Bridge-to-bridge calls: VHF 13 in most areas
International: radio doesn’t replace required whistle signals

slides.script: Inland rules also say a vessel that reaches agreement on a passing by radiotelephone is not obliged to sound the whistle signals, though she may. If agreement isn’t reached, whistle signals shall be exchanged in a timely manner, and they prevail. Bridge-to-bridge calls are usually on VHF channel thirteen. Under International rules there is no such exemption, so the whistle signals of Rule thirty-four are still required when you maneuver, whatever has been said on the radio. And under either set of rules, if you are in doubt about the other vessel’s intentions, the danger signal is always available.

lessons.title: Fog signals, attention signals and distress

slides.heading: Rule 35: underway in restricted visibility

items: P
Power, making way
PP
Power, underway but stopped
PSS
NUC, RAM, CBD, sail, fishing, towing
PSSS
Manned vessel being towed

slides.script: Rule thirty-five covers sound signals in or near an area of restricted visibility, by day or night. Underway, signals are sounded at intervals of not more than two minutes. A power-driven vessel making way through the water sounds one prolonged blast. A power-driven vessel underway but stopped sounds two prolonged blasts, with about two seconds between them. A vessel not under command, restricted, constrained by her draft, sailing, engaged in fishing, or towing or pushing sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts. A vessel towed, or the last vessel of a tow, if manned, sounds one prolonged followed by three short blasts, right after the towing vessel’s signal if practicable. A composite pushing unit gives the signals of a power-driven vessel.

A power-driven vessel making way through the water sounds one prolonged blast. A power-driven vessel underway but stopped sounds two prolonged blasts, with about two seconds between them. A vessel not under command, restricted, constrained by her draft, sailing, engaged in fishing, or towing or pushing sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts. A vessel towed, or the last vessel of a tow, if manned, sounds one prolonged followed by three short blasts, right after the towing vessel’s signal if practicable. A composite pushing unit gives the signals of a power-driven vessel.

slides.heading: At anchor and aground

head: Situation
Signal, at least every minute
rows: Bell forward, then gong aft, about 5 seconds each

slides.script: At anchor, the signals are given at intervals of not more than one minute. A vessel at anchor rings the bell rapidly for about five seconds. A vessel one hundred meters or more rings the bell in the fore part, then immediately sounds the gong rapidly for about five seconds in the after part. A vessel at anchor may also sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel. A vessel engaged in fishing at anchor, or a restricted vessel working at anchor, sounds one prolonged and two short instead of the anchor signals. A vessel aground gives the bell signal, plus the gong if required, with three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing.

A vessel at anchor may also sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel. A vessel engaged in fishing at anchor, or a restricted vessel working at anchor, sounds one prolonged and two short instead of the anchor signals. A vessel aground gives the bell signal, plus the gong if required, with three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing.

slides.heading: Small vessels and pilots

items: 12 to 20 m: bell signals not required at anchor or aground
If not given, make another efficient sound signal every 2 minutes
Under 12 m: Rule 35 signals not required, but an efficient sound signal every 2 minutes
Pilot vessel on duty may add four short blasts
Inland: under 20 m in a special anchorage area needs no anchor signal

slides.script: Smaller vessels get some relief. A vessel of twelve to twenty meters isn’t obliged to give the bell signals at anchor or aground, but if she doesn’t, she must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than two minutes. A vessel under twelve meters isn’t obliged to give any of the Rule thirty-five signals, but she must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than two minutes. A pilot vessel on pilotage duty may add an identity signal of four short blasts. And Inland, a vessel under twenty meters at anchor in a special anchorage area needn’t sound the anchor signal.

A pilot vessel on pilotage duty may add an identity signal of four short blasts. And Inland, a vessel under twenty meters at anchor in a special anchorage area needn’t sound the anchor signal.

slides.heading: Rule 36: attracting attention

items: Any light or sound that can’t be mistaken for a required signal
Or a searchlight aimed toward the danger, without embarrassing any vessel
Never use strobe or other high-intensity flashing lights

slides.script: Rule thirty-six lets any vessel attract the attention of another by making light or sound signals that cannot be mistaken for any signal authorized elsewhere in the rules, or by directing the beam of her searchlight in the direction of the danger, in such a way as not to embarrass any vessel. A light used to attract attention should not be mistaken for an aid to navigation. High-intensity intermittent or revolving lights, such as strobe lights, shall be avoided for this purpose. Embarrass here means dazzle or interfere with another vessel’s crew, so never aim a searchlight into a wheelhouse.

A light used to attract attention should not be mistaken for an aid to navigation. High-intensity intermittent or revolving lights, such as strobe lights, shall be avoided for this purpose. Embarrass here means dazzle or interfere with another vessel’s crew, so never aim a searchlight into a wheelhouse.

slides.heading: Rule 37 and Annex IV: distress signals

items: Gun or explosive signal about every minute
Continuous sounding of any fog-signal apparatus
Red star rockets or shells, one at a time
SOS by any method; “Mayday” by voice radio
Code flags N over C; a square flag with a ball above or below it
Flames on the vessel; red parachute or hand flares; orange smoke
Slowly raising and lowering outstretched arms
DSC distress alert, EPIRB, dye marker

slides.script: Rule thirty-seven says that when a vessel is in distress and requires assistance, she shall use or exhibit the signals described in Annex four. They are: a gun or other explosive signal fired at intervals of about a minute; a continuous sounding with any fog-signal apparatus; rockets or shells throwing red stars fired one at a time at short intervals; the signal SOS by any signaling method; the spoken word Mayday by radio; the code flags November Charlie; a square flag with a ball, or anything like a ball, above or below it; flames on the vessel; a rocket parachute flare or hand flare showing a red light; orange smoke; slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering arms outstretched to each side; a digital selective calling distress alert; an EPIRB signal; and a dye marker.

They are: a gun or other explosive signal fired at intervals of about a minute; a continuous sounding with any fog-signal apparatus; rockets or shells throwing red stars fired one at a time at short intervals; the signal SOS by any signaling method; the spoken word Mayday by radio; the code flags November Charlie; a square flag with a ball, or anything like a ball, above or below it; flames on the vessel; a rocket parachute flare or hand flare showing a red light; orange smoke; slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering arms outstretched to each side; a digital selective calling distress alert; an EPIRB signal; and a dye marker.

slides.heading: Distress: Inland and misuse

items: Inland adds: high-intensity white light flashing 50 to 70 times a minute
Use distress signals only to show distress and need of help
Don’t use signals that could be confused with them
Exam favorite: which of these is NOT a distress signal?

slides.script: Inland rules add one more distress signal: a high-intensity white light flashing at regular intervals from fifty to seventy times per minute. Using any of these signals except to indicate distress and need of assistance is prohibited, as is using any signal that might be confused with them. A favorite exam question lists four signals and asks which one is not a distress signal. Watch for traps like three short blasts, a green flare, or a white flare. Those aren’t distress signals. A continuously sounding fog horn is, and so is orange smoke.

lessons.title: Inland vs International, and bridge-to-bridge radio

slides.heading: Differences: sound signals

head: Topic
International
Inland
rows: Meeting or crossing within half a mile

slides.script: This final lesson pulls together the differences between Inland and International rules, because they produce a large share of exam questions. Start with sound signals. International maneuvering signals announce action being taken whenever a power-driven vessel maneuvers in sight of another. Inland signals propose an intention and need agreement between power-driven vessels meeting or crossing within half a mile. International overtaking signals are used in narrow channels and start with two prolonged blasts. Inland overtaking signals are one or two short blasts, in any waters. Inland, a radio agreement replaces the whistle signals, and a vessel leaving a berth sounds one prolonged blast. Inland maneuvering lights may be white or yellow.

slides.heading: Differences: vessels and lights

head: Topic
International
Inland
rows: All-round white may replace after masthead light and sternlight
Downbound has right of way; crossing vessel keeps clear
No anchor light or signal needed
White light flashing 50 to 70 per minute

slides.script: Now the differences in vessels and lights. Constrained by draft exists only in International rules. A vessel pushing ahead shows a sternlight under International rules, but two yellow towing lights Inland, and the barge she pushes carries a special flashing yellow light Inland. On the Great Lakes, an all-round white light may replace the after masthead light and sternlight. On the Great Lakes and Western Rivers, a downbound vessel with a following current has right of way, and a vessel crossing the river keeps clear. Inland, a vessel under twenty meters in a special anchorage area needs no anchor light, and a motorsailing vessel under twelve meters needn’t show the cone. Inland also adds the flashing white distress light.

slides.heading: The Bridge-to-Bridge Radiotelephone Act

items: Power-driven vessels 20 m and over
Vessels 100 gross tons and over carrying passengers for hire
Towing vessels 26 ft and over; dredges and floating plant near a channel
Keep a listening watch on VHF 13 in most areas, in English
Most six-packs aren’t required, but monitor 13 and 16 near ship channels

slides.script: The Vessel Bridge-to-Bridge Radiotelephone Act requires certain vessels on American waters to keep a listening watch on the designated bridge-to-bridge channel, which is VHF channel thirteen in most areas, so that captains can talk directly to each other. It applies to power-driven vessels of twenty meters or more, vessels of one hundred gross tons or more carrying one or more passengers for hire, towing vessels of twenty-six feet or more, and dredges and floating plant working in or near a channel. The person keeping the watch must be able to communicate in English. Most six-pack charter boats aren’t required to participate, but monitoring channels thirteen and sixteen near ship channels is good seamanship.

slides.heading: Position: latitude and longitude
slides.script: Welcome to Navigation General. This module covers how you know where the boat is and what the water and weather are doing, and it spans more topics than any other part of the exam. We start with position. Latitude measures distance north or south of the equator, from zero to ninety degrees. Longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian at Greenwich, from zero to one hundred eighty degrees. All of Florida is north latitude and west longitude. Each degree divides into sixty minutes. On the chart you read latitude on the side scales and longitude on the top and bottom scales, and a position is always written latitude first.
