slides.heading: The nautical mile and the knot

items: 1 minute of latitude = 1 nautical mile, about 6,076 ft
A statute mile is 5,280 ft; a nautical mile is about 15% longer
1 knot = 1 nautical mile per hour (never “knots per hour”)
A minute of longitude shrinks toward the poles: never measure distance with it

slides.script: One minute of latitude equals one nautical mile, about six thousand seventy-six feet, roughly fifteen percent longer than a statute mile. A knot is a speed of one nautical mile per hour, so never say knots per hour. Minutes of longitude are a nautical mile long only at the equator and get shorter toward the poles, which is why you never measure distance on the longitude scale. Modern charts and GPS units divide minutes into tenths, while older charts show seconds.

A knot is a speed of one nautical mile per hour, so never say knots per hour. Minutes of longitude are a nautical mile long only at the equator and get shorter toward the poles, which is why you never measure distance on the longitude scale. Modern charts and GPS units divide minutes into tenths, while older charts show seconds.

slides.heading: The Mercator projection

items: Most nautical charts use the Mercator projection
Straight lines are rhumb lines: constant direction
The latitude scale stretches toward the poles
Measure distance at the latitude where you’re working

slides.script: Most nautical charts use the Mercator projection. Its big advantage is that a straight line on the chart is a rhumb line, a line of constant direction, so you can lay a course with parallel rulers and steer it. The trade-off is distortion. The latitude scale gets longer as you move away from the equator, so on a small-scale chart a nautical mile measured near the top is longer than one measured near the bottom. That’s why you always measure distance on the part of the latitude scale beside where you’re working.

slides.heading: Chart scale and chart types

head: Chart type
Scale
Used for
rows: Strip and folio charts, like the ICW

slides.script: Chart scale is the ratio between a distance on the chart and the same distance on the earth. A scale of one to forty thousand is larger than one to eighty thousand, because each inch covers less ground and shows more detail. Remember: large scale, large detail, small area. NOAA groups charts into sailing charts for offshore passages, general charts for coastwise navigation, coast charts for inshore work, harbor charts for harbors and anchorages, and small-craft charts, such as the strip charts that follow the Intracoastal Waterway. Always use the largest-scale chart available for the waters you’re in.
slides.spoken: Chart scale is the ratio between a distance on the chart and the same distance on the earth. A scale of one to forty thousand is larger than one to eighty thousand, because each inch covers less ground and shows more detail. Remember: large scale, large detail, small area. NOAA groups charts into sailing charts for offshore passages, general charts for coastwise navigation, coast charts for inshore work, harbor charts for harbors and anchorages, and small-craft charts, such as the strip charts that follow the Intracoastal Waterway. Always use the largest-scale chart available for the waters you’re in.

slides.heading: Read the title block first

items: Chart number, title and scale
Soundings in feet, fathoms or meters, at mean lower low water
Horizontal datum: NAD 83, matching WGS 84 on your GPS
Heights and clearances above mean high water
Edition date: keep it corrected

slides.script: The title block is the first thing to read on any chart. It gives the chart number, title and scale; the units for soundings, which may be feet, fathoms or meters; the vertical datum for depths, usually mean lower low water; and the horizontal datum, normally the North American Datum of 1983, which for practical purposes matches the WGS 84 datum your GPS uses. If your plotter and chart use different datums, positions can be off. Heights of lights and landmarks and bridge clearances are measured above mean high water. Check the edition date too, and keep the chart corrected. NOAA is moving from traditional paper charts to electronic charts, so check what’s currently available for your area.

slides.heading: Chart colors

items: Buff or tan: land
Green: areas that cover and uncover with the tide
Blue: shallower water
White: deeper water
Magenta: lights, aids, cables and restricted areas

slides.script: Chart Number One, published by NOAA and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, explains every symbol and abbreviation on nautical charts, and the exam draws on it. Start with color. Land is buff or tan. Green marks areas that cover and uncover with the tide, like mud flats and oyster bars that dry at low water. Blue tints show shallower water, usually inside a chosen depth contour, and white shows deeper water. Magenta is used for lights, aids to navigation, cables, and restricted or regulated areas, so it draws your eye to things that matter.

slides.heading: Soundings, contours and the bottom

items: Soundings: depths below chart datum, usually MLLW
Depth contours join points of equal depth
Bottom: S sand, M mud, Sh shells, Rk rock, Co coral, G gravel
Qualifiers: hrd hard, sft soft, fne fine, crs coarse
Charted depths can be out of date, especially near inlets

slides.script: Soundings are the small numbers in the water, showing depth below the chart datum, usually mean lower low water. Depth contours are lines joining points of equal depth, so you can see a shoal or channel edge at a glance. Bottom characteristics are abbreviated: S for sand, M for mud, S h for shells, R k for rock, C o for coral, G for gravel, with qualifiers like h r d for hard and s f t for soft. These matter for anchoring, because sand and mud hold well while rock and coral don’t. Remember that charted depths may be old, and channels shoal, especially near Florida’s inlets.

slides.heading: Hazards

head: Symbol or note
Meaning
rows: Always above water; height above MHW
At the surface at chart datum
Hull symbol if visible, crossed lines if submerged
Position approximate, position doubtful, existence doubtful, reported

slides.script: Hazards have their own symbols. A rock that does not cover is always above water, with its height given above mean high water. A rock that covers and uncovers is exposed at low tide. A rock awash is right at the surface at chart datum. A sunken rock, marked with a cross, is always submerged and may be dangerous. Wrecks show as a hull symbol when visible and crossed lines when submerged. Watch for qualifiers: P A means position approximate, P D position doubtful, E D existence doubtful, and Rep means reported but not confirmed. Treat every one of them as real.

slides.heading: Regulated areas and landmarks

items: Anchorage and special anchorage areas
Cable and pipeline areas: no anchoring or dragging gear
Restricted areas, danger zones, security zones
Bridges: type, horizontal and vertical clearance
Landmarks: tanks, towers, stacks, spires

slides.script: Charts also show regulated areas, usually in magenta. Anchorage areas and special anchorage areas are outlined, and in a special anchorage area small vessels may anchor without anchor lights under Inland rules. Cable and pipeline areas mean don’t anchor or drag gear. Restricted areas, danger zones and security zones each have rules explained in the chart notes and the Coast Pilot. Bridges show their type and their horizontal and vertical clearances. Conspicuous landmarks like water tanks, radio towers, stacks and spires are useful for bearings, and a small circle on the symbol marks the exact position.

slides.heading: Chart notes and electronic charts

items: Read every note before using a chart
Notes cover regulations, cautions and datums
Raster charts: images of paper charts
ENCs: vector data; details can hide when zoomed out
Always use the most current edition

slides.script: Read every note printed on a chart before you navigate with it. Notes explain regulations, cautions about shoaling or unreliable aids, and datum information. On electronic charts you’ll see two kinds. Raster charts are scanned images of paper charts and look just like them. Electronic navigational charts, or E N Cs, are vector data that the plotter draws. They’re powerful, but soundings and hazards can disappear when you zoom out, so always zoom in to check your route. Whatever kind of chart you use, make sure it’s the most current edition.

slides.heading: Red, right, returning
slides.script: The United States uses IALA Region B, the buoyage system of the Americas, Japan, Korea and the Philippines. It is built on one phrase: red, right, returning. Returning means coming in from seaward, heading upstream, or, along the coast, traveling in the conventional direction, which runs clockwise around the country: south along the Atlantic coast, north up Florida’s Gulf coast, then west along the Gulf. Red buoys are nuns, with pointed tops, and carry even numbers. Green buoys are cans and carry odd numbers. Numbers increase heading inbound.

slides.heading: Lights on lateral marks

items: Red marks show red lights; green marks show green lights
Rhythms: flashing, occulting, quick, isophase
Quick flashing: sharp turn, junction or special caution
Lighted buoys are pillars or spars: read color and number
Preferred channel: composite group flashing (2+1)

slides.script: Lighted lateral buoys usually aren’t nun or can shaped. They’re pillar or spar buoys, so you identify them by color, number and light. A red mark shows a red light and a green mark shows a green light. Lateral lights use flashing, occulting, quick or isophase rhythms. A quick-flashing light often marks a sharp turn, a junction, or a spot needing special caution. A preferred channel mark shows a composite group-flashing light, two flashes followed by one, in the color of its top band. Unlighted buoys carry reflective tape in the mark’s color, so a spotlight at night can identify them.

slides.heading: Daybeacons

items: Fixed dayboards on piles
Red triangles, even numbers: keep on your right returning
Green squares, odd numbers: keep on your left returning
More reliable in position than buoys
Often in shallow water: don’t cut close

slides.script: Daybeacons are fixed aids, dayboards mounted on piles, common in Florida bays and along the Intracoastal Waterway. Red daybeacons are triangles with even numbers, and green daybeacons are squares with odd numbers, following the same red right returning rule. Because daybeacons are fixed, they’re more reliable in position than buoys. But they often stand in shallow water right at the edge of a channel, so give them a reasonable berth rather than cutting close.

slides.heading: Ranges
slides.script: A range is a pair of fixed marks, the front one lower and closer, the rear one higher and farther away, placed so that when they line up you’re on the centerline of a channel. Range dayboards are rectangular, often with a vertical stripe, and they may be lighted. If the rear mark appears to the right of the front mark, you’re left of the centerline, so steer right until they line up again. Remember: follow the rear mark. Ranges are also excellent for checking your compass, because the chart gives the range line’s true direction. Only follow a range within the charted channel, since the line can extend beyond safe water.

slides.heading: Don’t trust buoys blindly

items: Buoys can drag, sink, capsize or be off station
Lights can fail and colors fade
Use buoys as a guide, not a fixed position
Report discrepancies to the Coast Guard
Private aids (PATONs) follow the same colors and shapes

slides.script: Buoys are anchored floating objects. They can drag off station in storms, be struck by vessels, sink, or have their lights fail. The Light List warns mariners not to rely on buoys alone for position. Use them as a guide, and cross-check with charted features, depths and GPS. If you find an aid off station or not working, report it to the Coast Guard. Private aids to navigation, called PATONs, are placed by private owners like marinas. They must follow the same color and shape rules, but they may not be maintained to Coast Guard standards.

lessons.title: Other marks, the ICW and state markers

slides.heading: Non-lateral marks
slides.script: Some marks don’t tell you which side of a channel to pass. A safe water mark has red and white vertical stripes, often a red ball topmark, and a white light flashing Morse code A. It means open water all around, often the start of a channel. An isolated danger mark is black with red bands, with two black balls on top and a white light flashing in groups of two. It sits right on a small hazard with navigable water around it. A preferred channel mark has horizontal bands, and you treat it as the color of its top band. Yellow special marks show anchorages, cable areas, spoil areas and similar features.

slides.heading: The Intracoastal Waterway
slides.script: The Intracoastal Waterway is a big part of Florida boating. Its marks carry a yellow stripe, triangle or square. A yellow triangle means treat the mark as red. A yellow square means treat it as green, no matter what color the mark itself is. That matters where the waterway crosses an inlet channel and shares its buoys. On the waterway, returning means traveling clockwise around the country: south along the Atlantic coast, then north and west along the Gulf. In Florida, the waterway runs the length of the Atlantic coast and along long stretches of the Gulf coast.

slides.heading: State waterway markers
slides.script: Inland lakes, rivers and many state waters use regulatory markers from the Uniform State Waterway Marking System. They’re white with orange symbols. An orange diamond warns of danger, such as a rock or shoal, with the hazard described in black letters. A diamond with a cross inside means boats keep out, such as a swimming area or dam. An orange circle marks a controlled area, such as a speed limit, idle speed or no-wake zone, very common in Florida’s manatee zones. An orange square gives information, such as directions. A white buoy with a blue horizontal band is a mooring buoy.

slides.heading: The Western Rivers system

items: Buoys aren’t numbered: channels shift
Mileage boards show statute miles along the river
Passing daymarks: red triangles and green squares
Crossing daymarks: diamonds where the channel crosses the river

slides.script: The Western Rivers use a modified lateral system. Buoys there aren’t numbered, because channels shift with the river. Shore-mounted mileage boards show the distance in statute miles from a fixed point. Passing daymarks, red triangles and green squares, mark the side of the channel along a bank, and diamond-shaped crossing daymarks show where the channel crosses from one bank to the other. You may never see these from Florida, but the exam can ask about them.

slides.heading: Summary: marks and their lights
slides.script: Here’s a summary to memorize. Starboard-side lateral marks are red with red lights, and port-side marks are green with green lights. Preferred channel marks have red and green bands and a composite group-flashing light in the color of the top band. Safe water marks have red and white vertical stripes and a white Morse A light. Isolated danger marks are black with red bands and a white light flashing in groups of two. Special marks are yellow, with yellow lights. If you know this table, you can identify nearly any mark the exam describes.

lessons.title: Lights and how far you can see them

slides.heading: Light characteristics
slides.script: Every lighted aid has a characteristic, the pattern that identifies it. Fixed means steady. Flashing means the light is dark longer than lit. Quick means about sixty flashes a minute. Isophase means equal light and dark. Occulting means lit longer than dark, with brief eclipses. Group flashing shows flashes in groups. Morse A shows a short and a long. A chart label like F L two, white, ten seconds, forty-five feet, fourteen miles means a white light flashing two at a time every ten seconds, forty-five feet above mean high water, with a nominal range of fourteen nautical miles. Time the period with a watch to confirm which light you’re looking at.

slides.heading: The Light List

items: Every Coast Guard light, buoy and daybeacon in a region
Characteristic, height, nominal range, structure, remarks
Sector bearings and fog signals in the remarks
Volume III: Florida’s Atlantic coast through the Big Bend
Volume IV: the rest of the Gulf coast to Texas

slides.script: The Light List, published by the Coast Guard, describes every aid in its region: name and position, light characteristic, height above water, nominal range, the structure, and remarks such as sector bearings or fog signals. It’s divided into seven volumes. Volume three covers the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Little River, South Carolina, around Florida to the Econfina River in the Big Bend, so it includes most of Florida. Volume four continues along the Gulf to Texas. Check the Local Notice to Mariners for changes since the edition you’re using.

slides.heading: Nominal, luminous and geographic range

head: Range
Meaning
rows: How far the light carries in clear weather (10 nm meteorological visibility); shown on the chart
How far it carries in tonight’s actual visibility
How far before the earth’s curve hides it
The lesser of luminous and geographic range

slides.script: Three ranges describe how far a light can be seen. Nominal range is the distance a light carries in clear weather, defined as a meteorological visibility of ten nautical miles. That’s the number on the chart and in the Light List. Luminous range is how far the light carries in the visibility actually present tonight, which you find with the luminous range diagram in the Light List. Geographic range is how far you could see the light before the curve of the earth hides it, which depends on the light’s height and your height of eye. The distance at which you’ll actually first see the light is the lesser of the luminous range and the geographic range.

That’s the number on the chart and in the Light List. Geographic range is how far you could see the light before the curve of the earth hides it, which depends on the light’s height and your height of eye. The distance at which you’ll actually first see the light is the lesser of the luminous range and the geographic range.

slides.heading: Computing geographic range
slides.script: To find geographic range, find the distance to the horizon from the light and from your eye, and add them. The distance to the horizon in nautical miles is one point one seven times the square root of the height in feet. For a light sixty-four feet high, the square root is eight, so its horizon is about nine point four miles. For your eye at nine feet, the square root is three, so your horizon is about three and a half miles. Add them, and the geographic range is about twelve point nine miles. If the light’s luminous range tonight is fifteen miles, you’ll still only see it at about twelve point nine miles, because the lesser range wins.

slides.heading: Worked example

lines: Light height 100 ft; your eye 16 ft
Light’s horizon: 1.17 × √100 = 11.7 nm
Your horizon: 1.17 × √16 = 4.7 nm
Geographic range: 11.7 + 4.7 = 16.4 nm
Luminous range tonight 12 nm: you’ll see it at about 12 nm

slides.script: Let’s work one more. A light stands one hundred feet above the water, and your eye is sixteen feet up on a flybridge. The square root of one hundred is ten, and ten times one point one seven gives about eleven point seven miles. The square root of sixteen is four, and four times one point one seven gives about four point seven miles. The geographic range is the sum, about sixteen point four miles. But if tonight’s visibility limits the luminous range to twelve miles, you’ll only see the light at about twelve miles. The lesser range always wins.

slides.heading: Sector lights
slides.script: Some lights have colored sectors. A red sector usually covers a hazard, such as a shoal or reef, so if you see the light turn red, you’re standing into danger and should move back into the white sector. The Light List gives sector boundaries in degrees true, as seen from a vessel looking toward the light, not from the light outward. That’s a common exam trap. You can also use the moment a light first appears over the horizon, called bobbing a light, to estimate your distance off by comparing it with the geographic range.

slides.heading: The Coast Pilot

items: NOAA’s U.S. Coast Pilot: what the chart can’t show
Regulations, hazards, anchorages, bridges, currents, weather, ports
Coast Pilot 4: Cape Henry, VA to Key West
Coast Pilot 5: Gulf coast, Puerto Rico and Virgin Islands
Free to download; updated regularly

slides.script: The United States Coast Pilot, published by NOAA, supplements the chart with information that can’t be drawn on it: navigation regulations, local hazards, anchorages, bridge and cable clearances, currents, weather, and descriptions of ports and channels. It comes in nine volumes. Coast Pilot four covers the Atlantic coast from Cape Henry, Virginia, to Key West, and Coast Pilot five covers the Gulf coast, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Read the relevant chapters before you run a new inlet or harbor. It’s free to download and updated regularly.

slides.heading: Notices to Mariners

items: Local Notice to Mariners: weekly, from each Coast Guard district
Aid changes and discrepancies, dredging, hazards, events, chart corrections
NGA Notice to Mariners: weekly, for ocean charts
Broadcast Notices: urgent info, announced on VHF 16, read on 22A

slides.script: Notices to Mariners keep your charts and publications current. The Local Notice to Mariners is published weekly by each Coast Guard district. It covers aids that have been added, moved or are off station, dredging and construction, marine events, hazards, and chart corrections for local waters. The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency publishes a weekly Notice to Mariners for ocean charts and international publications. For urgent information, the Coast Guard makes Broadcast Notices to Mariners, announced on VHF channel sixteen and then read on channel twenty-two alpha.

You already know the Navigation Rules handbook and Chart Number One. The Code of Federal Regulations contains the laws you operate under. Title thirty-three covers navigation and navigable waters. Title forty-six covers shipping, including uninspected passenger vessels and your license.

slides.heading: Keeping charts corrected

items: Note the chart’s edition date
Check every Local Notice issued since then
Mark corrections neatly and log them
Chartplotters: install chart updates regularly
When sources disagree, use the newest and go carefully

slides.script: Correcting charts is a basic duty. Start with the edition date of your chart, then check every Local Notice to Mariners issued since that date for corrections that affect it. On paper charts, mark corrections neatly and record them in a correction log, so you know the chart is up to date. On chartplotters, install chart updates regularly, since an old memory card can be years out of date. When sources disagree, use the most recent information and navigate with extra caution.

slides.heading: Types of tide
slides.script: Tides are caused mainly by the moon’s gravity, with help from the sun. There are three types. A semidiurnal tide has two high and two low waters each day of roughly equal height, like Florida’s Atlantic coast. A mixed tide has two highs and two lows of noticeably unequal height, common along much of Florida’s Gulf coast. A diurnal tide has just one high and one low each day, as in parts of the Panhandle. Because the tidal day is about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, high and low water come roughly fifty minutes later each day.

slides.heading: Tide terms

items: Range: the difference between high and low water
Depths from MLLW; heights and clearances from MHW
Actual depth = charted depth + height of tide
Negative tide: water below MLLW, shallower than charted
Stand: the pause at high or low water

slides.script: A few terms. High water and low water are the highest and lowest levels in each tide cycle, and the range is the difference between them. Charted depths are measured from mean lower low water, so the actual depth at any moment equals the charted depth plus the height of tide. A tide height can be negative, meaning the water is below mean lower low water and shallower than charted. That happens around spring tides, especially with strong offshore winds. The stand of the tide is the brief period at high or low water when the level barely changes.

slides.heading: Spring and neap tides
slides.script: The range of the tide follows the moon. At new and full moon, the sun and moon line up and you get spring tides, with the biggest range. Spring has nothing to do with the season. At the first and third quarter moons, the sun and moon pull at right angles and you get neap tides, with the smallest range. When a spring tide coincides with the moon’s closest approach to the earth, perigean spring tides, often called king tides, flood low-lying Florida streets. Wind and weather matter too. Strong onshore winds and low pressure raise water levels, and offshore winds lower them.

slides.heading: How the Tide Tables work

head: Table
What it gives
rows: Daily high and low times and heights at reference stations
Corrections for subordinate stations: time differences, and height differences or ratios
Height of tide at any time between high and low

slides.script: The classic Tide Tables used on the exam have three main tables. Table one gives the daily times and heights of high and low water at reference stations. Table two lists subordinate stations, each tied to a reference station, with time differences for high and low water and height corrections. Height corrections are either a number of feet to add or subtract, or a ratio, marked with an asterisk, that you multiply by the reference heights. Table three lets you find the height of tide at any time between high and low water. Times are in local standard time, so add one hour during daylight saving time.

slides.heading: Worked example: subordinate station

lines: Reference: high 10:42, 3.6 ft; low 16:50, 0.4 ft
Subordinate: high +0:35, +0.4 ft; low +0:48, −0.1 ft
Daylight saving time: add 1 hour, giving 12:17 and 18:38

slides.script: Let’s work a subordinate station. The reference station predicts high water at ten forty-two, three point six feet, and low water at sixteen fifty, zero point four feet. The subordinate station’s corrections are plus thirty-five minutes and plus zero point four feet for high water, and plus forty-eight minutes and minus zero point one feet for low water. So high water at the subordinate station is at eleven seventeen, four point zero feet, and low water is at seventeen thirty-eight, zero point three feet. In summer, with daylight saving time in effect, add one hour: twelve seventeen and eighteen thirty-eight.

slides.heading: Height of tide at a given time

lines: Low 0.5 ft at 06:00, high 6.5 ft at 12:00: range 6 ft
At 09:00, three hours in: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6/12 of the range
6/12 × 6 ft = 3 ft above low water
Height of tide at 09:00 ≈ 0.5 + 3 = 3.5 ft
Charted 5 ft spot: about 8.5 ft of water at 09:00

slides.script: To estimate the height of tide between high and low, use the rule of twelfths or Table three. Say low water is zero point five feet at six hundred hours and high water is six point five feet at noon, a range of six feet over six hours. By nine hundred, three hours in, the tide has risen one plus two plus three twelfths, which is six twelfths, or half the range: three feet. Add that to the low water height, and the tide is about three point five feet. Where the chart shows five feet, you’ll have about eight and a half feet of water at nine hundred.

slides.heading: Tidal currents

items: Current is named for where it flows TOWARD (its set)
Wind is named for where it comes FROM
Flood toward land, ebb away, slack between
Reversing currents in channels; rotary currents offshore
Slack often doesn’t match high or low tide

slides.script: Tidal current is the horizontal flow of water caused by the tide. A current is named for the direction it flows toward, called its set, while wind is named for the direction it comes from. So a north wind blows toward the south, but a north-setting current flows toward the north. That difference shows up on the exam. Flood current flows toward land, ebb away from it, and slack water is the brief period between. In rivers and inlets currents reverse direction, while offshore they may be rotary, turning steadily around the compass. Slack water often doesn’t coincide with high or low tide, especially in inlets, so never assume one from the other.

slides.heading: The Tidal Current Tables

head: Table
What it gives
rows: Daily times of slack and maximum current, with max speeds, at reference stations
Subordinate stations: time differences, speed ratios, flood and ebb directions
Current speed at any time between slack and maximum

slides.script: The Tidal Current Tables work like the Tide Tables. Table one gives daily times of slack water and maximum current at reference stations, with maximum flood and ebb speeds. Table two gives corrections for subordinate stations: time differences for slack and maximum current, speed ratios for flood and ebb, and the true directions of flood and ebb. Table three gives the current speed at any time between slack and maximum. For example, if the reference station predicts a maximum flood of two knots at fourteen hundred, and a subordinate station has a time difference of minus twenty minutes and a flood ratio of point six, expect a maximum flood of one point two knots at thirteen forty.

slides.heading: Florida’s big currents

items: The Florida Current (Gulf Stream) flows north along the east coast
Often 2 to 4 knots or more; closest to shore off Palm Beach County
North wind against the Stream: steep, dangerous seas
The Loop Current in the Gulf feeds it
Inlets: strong ebb against an onshore wind breaks

slides.script: Florida captains deal with one of the strongest ocean currents in the world. The Florida Current, the beginning of the Gulf Stream, flows north along the east coast, often at two to four knots and sometimes more, and it comes closest to shore off Palm Beach County. When a strong north wind blows against the northbound Stream, seas become short, steep and dangerous, so experienced captains don’t cross in a norther. In the Gulf, the Loop Current feeds the Florida Current. Closer in, a strong ebb running out of an inlet against an onshore wind can produce breaking seas right in the entrance.

slides.heading: Course to steer in a current
slides.script: Current sailing means finding a course to steer that cancels a known current. Draw your intended track from your position to your destination. From your starting point, draw the current vector, its set and its drift for one hour. Then, from the end of the current vector, swing an arc equal to your boat speed until it crosses the intended track. The line from the end of the current vector to that crossing point is your course to steer. The distance from your start to the crossing point along the track is your speed made good. You’ll practice this in the plotting module.

The line from the end of the current vector to that crossing point is your course to steer. The distance from your start to the crossing point along the track is your speed made good. slides.heading: Measuring the current from fixes

lines: 08:00 fix; plot your 10:00 DR from course and speed
10:00 fix lies 3 nm from the 10:00 DR, bearing 150°T
Set = 150°T, the direction from DR to fix
Drift = 3 nm ÷ 2 hours = 1.5 knots
Use it to correct your next course

slides.script: When you don’t know the current in advance, you can measure it. Plot your dead reckoning position from course and speed, then take a fix. The current’s set is the direction from your DR position to your fix, and its drift is the distance between them divided by the time since your last fix. For example, if your ten hundred fix lies three nautical miles from your ten hundred DR position, bearing one five zero true, and your last fix was at eight hundred, the set is one five zero true and the drift is one and a half knots. This also captures the effects of wind and steering error.

slides.heading: The compass itself

items: A magnetized card floats in liquid and points to magnetic north
The lubber line marks the boat’s heading
Mount it on or parallel to the centerline
Keep magnets, electronics, speakers and tools away
Gimbals keep it level as the boat rolls

slides.script: The magnetic compass is the one navigation instrument that needs no electricity. A magnetized card floats in liquid and aligns itself with the earth’s magnetic field. The lubber line, a mark on the compass bowl, is aligned with the boat’s centerline, and your heading is the number on the card at the lubber line. Mount the compass on or parallel to the centerline where the helmsman can see it, and keep magnetic and electrical items away from it: speakers, radios, phones, tools, even a drink holder with a magnet. Moving any of these can change your compass error.

slides.heading: True, magnetic, compass
slides.script: There are three ways to express a direction: true, magnetic and compass. Variation is the difference between true and magnetic. Deviation is the difference between magnetic and compass. Remember the order with the phrase True Virgins Make Dull Companions: true, variation, magnetic, deviation, compass. Going from compass toward true is called correcting, and you add easterly errors and subtract westerly ones. Going from true toward compass is called uncorrecting, and you do the opposite: add westerly errors and subtract easterly ones. Another memory aid for correcting is Can Dead Men Vote Twice At Elections: compass, deviation, magnetic, variation, true, add east.

slides.heading: Variation

items: Caused by Earth’s magnetic field; the same on every heading
Read it from the chart’s compass rose
Update for annual change to the current year
Florida: roughly 2° to 8° west, depending on location
Westerly variation: magnetic north lies west of true north

slides.script: Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at your location. It’s the same no matter which way the boat is heading. Read it from the center of the nearest compass rose on your chart, which also gives the year it was measured and the annual change. Multiply the annual change by the number of years since then, and apply it. In Florida, variation is a few degrees west, from roughly two degrees in the western Panhandle to around eight degrees on the Atlantic coast, and it changes slowly over time. Westerly variation means magnetic north lies to the west of true north.

slides.heading: Deviation

items: Caused by your boat’s own magnetism
Changes as the boat’s heading changes
Recorded on a deviation card for each heading
Use the deviation for your HEADING, even when taking a bearing
“Compass least, error east; compass best, error west”

slides.script: Deviation is the error caused by your boat’s own magnetic fields. Unlike variation, it changes as your heading changes, so it’s recorded on a deviation card listing the error for each heading. Here’s a key exam point. When you take a compass bearing of a landmark, you correct it using the deviation for the boat’s heading, not the direction of the bearing, because deviation depends on how the boat is pointed. And a handy rule for naming the error: compass least, error east; compass best, error west. If the compass reads less than magnetic, deviation is east.

slides.heading: Worked example: correcting a bearing

lines: Heading 045° by compass; deviation on 045° is 2°W; variation 5°W
Lighthouse bears 120° by compass
120° − 2° (deviation for your heading) = 118° magnetic
118° − 5° (variation) = 113° true
Plot the bearing as 113°T

slides.script: Here’s that bearing trap worked out. You’re steering zero four five by compass, and your deviation card shows two degrees west on that heading. Variation is five degrees west. You take a compass bearing on a lighthouse and read one two zero. Use the deviation for your heading, two west, not the deviation for one two zero. Correcting toward true, subtract west: one two zero minus two is one one eight magnetic, and one one eight minus five is one one three true. Bearings are always plotted on the chart as true, so you’d plot one one three.

lessons.title: Headings, bearings and checking the compass

slides.heading: Navigation words

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Direction the bow points right now
Direction you actually move over the bottom
Speed actually made over the bottom
Direction from you to an object

slides.script: Navigators use precise words. Heading is the direction the bow is pointing at this moment, which wanders as the boat yaws. Course is the direction you intend to steer. Track, or course over ground on a GPS, is the direction the boat actually moves over the bottom, which differs from heading when wind and current push you sideways. Speed over ground is your actual speed over the bottom, as opposed to speed through the water. A bearing is the direction from your boat to an object, and it can be true, magnetic, compass or relative.

Speed over ground is your actual speed over the bottom, as opposed to speed through the water. slides.heading: Relative bearings
slides.script: A relative bearing is measured clockwise from the bow: zero zero zero dead ahead, zero nine zero on the starboard beam, one eight zero astern, and two seven zero on the port beam. To convert a relative bearing to a true bearing, add it to your true heading, and subtract three hundred sixty if the total goes over three hundred sixty. For example, with a true heading of three hundred, an object bearing zero nine zero relative is at zero three zero true. Lookouts often report this way: broad on the starboard bow means about forty-five degrees relative.

For example, with a true heading of three hundred, an object bearing zero nine zero relative is at zero three zero true. slides.heading: Using a deviation table
slides.script: A deviation table lists the error for each heading. Find your heading in the table, and if it falls between two entries, interpolate. Using this table, a magnetic heading of zero seven five falls halfway between zero six zero, with no deviation, and zero nine zero, with two degrees west, so the deviation is about one degree west. Some tables are arranged by compass heading and some by magnetic heading, so check which you’re using. Exam questions often give you a table like this and ask for the deviation or the compass course to steer.

slides.heading: Checking your compass

items: Line up on a range and compare with its charted direction
The difference is your deviation on that heading
GPS course over ground is a rough check in calm, slack water
Swinging ship: check all headings and record them
Recheck after installing electronics or moving gear

slides.script: Check your compass regularly. The easiest way is with a range. Lined up on a range, compare your compass reading with the range’s magnetic direction from the chart, and the difference is your deviation on that heading. You can also compare your compass heading with GPS course over ground in calm conditions with no current, though that’s less precise. Checking the compass on all headings and recording the results is called swinging ship. A compass adjuster can reduce deviation with small corrector magnets. Recheck whenever you install new electronics or move gear near the compass.

slides.heading: Worked example: a range check

lines: Range line on the chart: 042°T
Variation 6°W: 042° + 6° = 048° magnetic
On the range, your compass reads 051°
Compass reads 3° more than magnetic: deviation 3°W
“Compass best, error west”

slides.script: Let’s check a compass on a range. The chart shows the range line at zero four two true. Variation is six west, and going from true toward magnetic you add west, so the magnetic direction is zero four eight. Lined up on the range, your compass reads zero five one. The compass reads three degrees more than magnetic, so the deviation on this heading is three degrees west. Compass best, error west. Record it on your deviation card for that heading.

Variation is six west, and going from true toward magnetic you add west, so the magnetic direction is zero four eight. Lined up on the range, your compass reads zero five one. The compass reads three degrees more than magnetic, so the deviation on this heading is three degrees west. Compass best, error west. Record it on your deviation card for that heading.

slides.heading: GPS

items: Satellite positioning, typically accurate to a few meters
WAAS corrections improve accuracy
Speed and course over ground come from position changes
Set the datum to match your chart
GPS can fail or be jammed: keep backup skills

slides.script: GPS gives your position from satellite signals, typically accurate to within a few meters, and better with WAAS, a correction system available across North America. A GPS receiver also gives speed over ground and course over ground, which come from changes in position, not from the compass. Make sure the receiver’s datum matches your chart, normally WGS 84 matched to NAD 83. GPS can fail, lose power or be jammed, so a good captain keeps dead reckoning skills, paper charts and a compass as backups. The Loran system that once backed up GPS was shut down in 2010.

slides.heading: Chartplotters

items: Your GPS position on an electronic chart
Waypoints and routes: check every leg for hazards
Cross-track error: distance off your intended track
Zoom in to see all detail on vector charts
Keep charts updated; never rely on one source

slides.script: A chartplotter shows your GPS position on an electronic chart. You can enter waypoints and build routes, but before you follow a route, zoom in and check every leg for shoals, markers and obstructions, because a straight line between waypoints may cross a shoal or even land. Cross-track error shows how far you are to the side of your intended track. Vector charts may hide details when zoomed out. The Coast Guard and the courts expect a prudent captain not to rely solely on any single aid, so cross-check the plotter with buoys, depths and visual bearings.

You can enter waypoints and build routes, but before you follow a route, zoom in and check every leg for shoals, markers and obstructions, because a straight line between waypoints may cross a shoal or even land. Cross-track error shows how far you are to the side of your intended track. Vector charts may hide details when zoomed out. The Coast Guard and the courts expect a prudent captain not to rely solely on any single aid, so cross-check the plotter with buoys, depths and visual bearings.

slides.heading: AIS

items: Automatic Identification System: VHF data broadcasts
Name, MMSI, position, course, speed; CPA on your plotter
Class A: larger commercial vessels; Class B: smaller boats
Many vessels don’t carry AIS: keep a lookout
AIS contact isn’t “in sight” under the Rules

slides.script: The Automatic Identification System, or AIS, broadcasts a vessel’s identity, position, course and speed over VHF data channels. With an AIS receiver you can see a ship’s name and call her directly, and your plotter can calculate the closest point of approach. Class A transponders are required on many commercial vessels, and Class B units are designed for smaller boats. Many vessels carry no AIS at all, so it never replaces a proper lookout. And seeing a vessel on AIS doesn’t mean you’re in sight of her under the Navigation Rules.

slides.heading: Depth sounder

items: Measures depth below the transducer
Set an offset for depth below the keel or waterline
Compare with charted depth plus tide to confirm position
Follow a depth contour in poor visibility
Use a shallow-water alarm

slides.script: The depth sounder sends a sound pulse down and times its echo. It shows depth below the transducer, unless you’ve set an offset to show depth below the keel or below the waterline, so know how yours is set. Depth is a powerful navigation check. Compare your reading with the charted depth plus the height of tide to confirm your position, and in poor visibility you can follow a depth contour toward a harbor. Set a shallow-water alarm as a safety net, especially in Florida’s skinny water.

slides.heading: VHF and DSC

items: Range is roughly line of sight: antenna height matters
16: distress, safety and calling; 9: recreational calling
13: bridge-to-bridge; 22A: Coast Guard working
DSC: register an MMSI and connect GPS
WX channels: NOAA Weather Radio, 162.400 to 162.550 MHz

slides.script: Your VHF radio is also a navigation tool. Its range is roughly line of sight, so antenna height matters more than power. Channel sixteen is for distress, safety and calling. Channel nine is an alternate calling channel for recreational boats. Channel thirteen is the bridge-to-bridge channel, and channel twenty-two alpha is the Coast Guard working channel. A DSC radio needs a registered MMSI number and a GPS connection to send your position in a distress alert. The weather channels carry continuous NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts.

slides.heading: How radar works
slides.script: Radar transmits pulses of microwave energy and measures the time for echoes to return. It measures range very accurately, and bearing somewhat less accurately, because the beam has width. On the display, your boat is usually at the center, with a heading line pointing up and range rings to help judge distance. The variable range marker, or V R M, measures range to a target, and the electronic bearing line, or E B L, measures its bearing. If a target stays on your E B L while its range closes, its bearing is steady, and Rule seven says risk of collision exists.

slides.heading: The key controls

items: Gain: overall sensitivity
Sea clutter (STC): reduces echoes from nearby waves
Rain clutter (FTC): breaks up rain returns
Too much clutter control erases real targets
Head-up, north-up and course-up displays

slides.script: Three controls matter most. Gain sets overall sensitivity: too low and you miss weak targets, too high and the screen fills with speckle. Sea clutter control reduces echoes from waves close to the boat. Rain clutter control breaks up the solid returns from rain. The danger is turning these controls up so far that real targets, like a small boat or a buoy, disappear. Displays can be head-up, with the heading line straight up, or north-up and course-up, which stabilize the picture using a heading sensor and make plotting easier.

slides.heading: Radar’s limits

items: Radar horizon is only a little beyond the visual horizon
Low beaches may not show: the first echo may be land inland
Small fiberglass, wood and rubber boats return weak echoes
Large objects cast shadows that hide targets
False echoes: side lobes, multiple echoes, second-trace returns

slides.script: Know radar’s limits. The radar horizon is only a little farther than the visual horizon, so a low target beyond it won’t show. A low sandy beach may give little return, and the first strong echo may come from higher land or buildings well inland, which can make you think you’re farther off than you are. Small fiberglass, wooden or rubber boats return weak echoes, which is why a radar reflector is worth carrying. Large ships and islands cast shadows that hide targets behind them. And radar can show false echoes, such as side-lobe echoes or multiple echoes between you and a nearby ship.

slides.heading: Plotting and CPA

items: Mark a target’s position several times
The line through them is its relative motion
CPA: closest point of approach; TCPA: time to it
MARPA or ARPA can track targets automatically
Rule 7: no decisions on scanty radar information

slides.script: To judge risk of collision on radar, mark a target’s position several times over a few minutes. The line through those marks is its relative motion line. Extend it past the center of the screen, and the closest distance between that line and your boat is the closest point of approach, or C P A. The time until you reach it is the T C P A. Many radars can track targets automatically, called MARPA on small boats or ARPA on ships, and compute C P A for you. Remember Rule seven: radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation is required, and decisions must not be based on scanty radar information, like a single glance at the screen.

slides.heading: Radar and the Rules

items: If fitted, radar must be used properly (Rule 7)
A radar-only contact isn’t “in sight” (Rule 3)
Rule 19: don’t turn to port for targets forward of the beam
A radar reflector helps others see you
Practice in clear weather before you need it in fog

slides.script: Radar ties directly into the Navigation Rules. If your boat has radar, Rule seven requires you to use it properly, including long-range scanning for early warning. A target seen only on radar is not in sight, so in fog Rule nineteen applies, and you avoid turning to port for a target forward of the beam. Make your own boat a better target with a radar reflector mounted as high as practical. And practice with radar on clear days, comparing the screen with what you see, so you can trust your interpretation when the fog rolls in.

slides.heading: Highs, lows and fronts
slides.script: Weather moves in systems. Air flows from high pressure toward low pressure, and the earth’s rotation bends it. In the Northern Hemisphere, winds blow clockwise and outward around a high, which usually brings fair weather, and counterclockwise and inward around a low, which brings clouds, wind and rain. A front is the boundary between air masses. A cold front, drawn with triangles, moves fast and brings a sharp line of showers or thunderstorms, a sudden wind shift, and then clearing, cooler weather. A warm front, drawn with semicircles, moves slowly and brings a long period of low clouds, drizzle and poor visibility ahead of it.

A front is the boundary between air masses. A cold front, drawn with triangles, moves fast and brings a sharp line of showers or thunderstorms, a sudden wind shift, and then clearing, cooler weather. A warm front, drawn with semicircles, moves slowly and brings a long period of low clouds, drizzle and poor visibility ahead of it.

slides.heading: Florida cold fronts

items: Ahead: southerly winds, falling barometer, building clouds
At the front: squall line, gusts, sudden wind shift
Behind: wind veers west, then northwest and north
Barometer rises; clear, cool, often rough for a day or two
East coast: north winds against the Gulf Stream

slides.script: In Florida, winter cold fronts set the rhythm of offshore fishing. Ahead of a front, winds blow from the south or southwest, the barometer falls, and clouds build. As the front passes, a squall line can bring gusty winds and rain, and the wind shifts suddenly. Behind it, the wind veers to the west, then northwest and north, often blowing hard for a day or two, while the barometer rises and the sky clears. On the Atlantic side, those north winds blow against the Gulf Stream and make it dangerous. The best fishing windows often come just before a front, or after the wind lies down behind it.

slides.heading: Reading the barometer and the sky

items: Falling barometer: low or front approaching
Rapid fall: strong wind soon
Rising barometer: improving weather
Cirrus thickening and lowering: warm front coming
Towering cumulus with anvil tops: thunderstorms
Buys Ballot: back to the wind, low on your left

slides.script: Your barometer and the sky give early warning. A falling barometer signals an approaching low or front, and a rapid fall means strong wind is coming soon. A rising barometer means improving weather. High, thin cirrus clouds that thicken and lower over several hours often mean a warm front is approaching. Towering cumulus clouds that grow into anvil-topped cumulonimbus mean thunderstorms. And remember Buys Ballot’s law: in the Northern Hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and low pressure is on your left.

slides.heading: Marine forecasts and warnings

head: Advisory or warning
Sustained wind
rows: Roughly 20 to 33 knots, or hazardous seas; thresholds vary by region
Short-lived hazards: thunderstorms, waterspouts, strong gusts

slides.script: Get the marine forecast before every trip. The National Weather Service issues coastal waters and offshore forecasts, available online and broadcast continuously on NOAA Weather Radio. Learn the warning levels. A small craft advisory is issued for winds roughly in the twenty to thirty-three knot range, or for hazardous seas, with exact thresholds varying by region. A gale warning means thirty-four to forty-seven knots. A storm warning means forty-eight to sixty-three knots. A hurricane force wind warning means sixty-four knots or more. A special marine warning covers short-lived hazards like severe thunderstorms and waterspouts.

slides.heading: The Beaufort scale
slides.script: The Beaufort scale describes wind force by its effect on the sea. Force zero is calm. Force three, a gentle breeze of seven to ten knots, brings scattered whitecaps. Force four, a moderate breeze of eleven to sixteen knots, brings frequent whitecaps. Force six, a strong breeze of twenty-two to twenty-seven knots, builds large waves with extensive foam crests, which is where many small charter boats stay at the dock. Force eight is a gale, thirty-four to forty knots, and force twelve is hurricane force, sixty-four knots and above.

slides.heading: Thunderstorms and waterspouts

items: Summer storms build over land in the afternoon and drift to the coast
Hear thunder? You’re within striking distance: head in
Outflow gusts can hit before the rain
Caught out: everyone low, away from metal, out of the water
Waterspouts: move away at right angles to their path

slides.script: Florida leads the nation in lightning, and summer thunderstorms are a near-daily hazard. They usually build over land in the early afternoon and drift toward the coast. Gusts flowing out of a storm can hit well before the rain, sometimes at gale force. If you hear thunder, you’re within striking distance, so head in early. If you’re caught out, get everyone low, away from metal, rods and the console, and out of the water. Waterspouts are common in the Keys and along both coasts. Most are fair-weather spouts, but treat every one as dangerous and move away at right angles to its path.

slides.heading: Tropical cyclones

head: Type
Sustained wind
rows: Category 3 and up: 96 knots and over

slides.script: Tropical cyclones are classified by sustained wind. A tropical depression has winds under thirty-four knots, a tropical storm thirty-four to sixty-three knots, and a hurricane sixty-four knots or more. Category three and higher hurricanes, ninety-six knots and above, are called major hurricanes. Atlantic hurricane season runs from June first through November thirtieth, with the peak from August through October. The National Hurricane Center issues a watch when hurricane conditions are possible, usually within forty-eight hours, and a warning when they are expected, usually within thirty-six hours.

slides.heading: The dangerous semicircle
slides.script: In the Northern Hemisphere, hurricane winds circulate counterclockwise. On the right side of the storm’s track, the storm’s forward motion adds to the wind speed, so this is called the dangerous semicircle, and the right front quadrant usually has the strongest winds and the highest storm surge. On the left side, forward motion subtracts from the wind, so it’s called the navigable semicircle, though it’s still extremely dangerous. For a charter captain, the real lesson is preparation. Have a written hurricane plan, know where you’ll secure or haul the boat, and act early, because bridges lock down and marinas fill up.

slides.heading: Fog

items: Advection fog: warm moist air moving over cooler water
Radiation fog: clear, calm nights; drifts over rivers and bays
Florida sea fog: mostly winter and spring
When visibility drops: Rule 19 and fog signals
Slow down, lights on, radar plotting, extra lookout

slides.script: Fog forms when air cools to its dew point. Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves over cooler water, and it can persist for hours or even days. In Florida, it’s most common in winter and spring, when warm air flows over cooler nearshore water. Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights as the land cools, and it can drift over rivers, bays and harbors until the morning sun burns it off. When visibility drops, follow Rule nineteen: slow to a safe speed, turn on your navigation lights, sound fog signals, plot radar targets and post an extra lookout.

slides.heading: Waves and seas

items: Wave size grows with wind speed, fetch and duration
Fetch: the distance of open water the wind blows across
Swell: waves that have left the area where they formed
Forecast heights are significant wave height: the average of the highest third
Expect some waves much larger, occasionally about double

slides.script: Waves grow with three things: wind speed; fetch, the distance of open water the wind blows across; and duration, how long it has blown. That’s why an offshore wind leaves a calm strip near the beach, while the same wind blowing onshore across a long fetch builds big seas. Swell is waves that have traveled away from where they formed, and it can arrive well ahead of a distant storm. Forecast wave heights are significant wave heights, the average of the highest one third of the waves, so expect some individual waves much larger, occasionally around twice the forecast height.

lessons.title: Your license and the passenger rules

slides.heading: What the OUPV allows

items: Up to 6 passengers for hire
On uninspected vessels
Near Coastal: up to 100 nm offshore; Inland: inside the boundary line
Valid 5 years; renew through the National Maritime Center
7 or more passengers: inspected vessel and a Master license

slides.script: Welcome to Deck General and Safety, the module about running a safe, legal operation. It starts with your license. An OUPV credential, the six-pack, lets you carry up to six passengers for hire on an uninspected vessel. A Near Coastal endorsement lets you operate up to one hundred miles offshore, while an Inland endorsement keeps you inside the boundary line. The credential is valid for five years, and you renew it through the National Maritime Center. To carry seven or more passengers for hire, you need an inspected vessel with a Certificate of Inspection, and a Master license.

The credential is valid for five years, and you renew it through the National Maritime Center. To carry seven or more passengers for hire, you need an inspected vessel with a Certificate of Inspection, and a Master license.

slides.heading: Who is a passenger for hire?

items: A passenger for whom consideration is contributed as a condition of carriage
Consideration: money or any economic benefit, directly or indirectly
Voluntary sharing of the trip’s actual expenses is NOT consideration
Owners, crew and true non-paying guests aren’t passengers for hire
Disguised fees (“donations,” required fuel charges) still count

slides.script: The key legal term is passenger for hire: a passenger for whom consideration is contributed as a condition of carriage, directly or indirectly. Consideration means money or any other economic benefit, inducement, right or profit. Federal law specifically excludes the voluntary sharing of a trip’s actual expenses, like friends splitting fuel and bait. But the moment payment becomes a condition of going, even disguised as a donation, a club membership or a mandatory fuel charge, those people are passengers for hire, and you need a licensed captain and a properly documented or registered boat.

But the moment payment becomes a condition of going, even disguised as a donation, a club membership or a mandatory fuel charge, those people are passengers for hire, and you need a licensed captain and a properly documented or registered boat.

slides.heading: Uninspected vs inspected vessels

head: Vessel
Passengers for hire
Credential
rows: More than 6, up to the limit on its COI
Charterer hires the boat and supplies the captain
Strict rules; a common illegal-charter disguise

slides.script: Here’s how the categories fit together. An uninspected passenger vessel may carry no more than six passengers for hire, and the operator needs at least an OUPV credential. Carrying more than six requires an inspected small passenger vessel, with a Certificate of Inspection that sets the maximum number of passengers, and a Master license. Bareboat charters, where the charterer hires the boat and supplies an independent captain, are tightly regulated. The Coast Guard regularly fines operators who use fake bareboat arrangements to run illegal charters, so be very careful with anything that looks like one.

slides.heading: The boat’s paperwork

items: 5 net tons or more, passengers for hire between U.S. points: Coast Guard documentation with a coastwise endorsement
Smaller boats: state registration
Florida: the right FWC charter fishing license covers your customers
Carry your credential, the boat’s papers and required placards aboard

slides.script: Your boat needs the right paperwork too. A boat of five net tons or more that carries passengers for hire between American points must be documented by the Coast Guard with a coastwise endorsement, which also has requirements about where the boat was built and who owns it. Smaller boats are registered with the state. In Florida, charter fishing operations also need the right saltwater fishing license from the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission so your customers are covered. Carry your credential, the boat’s documents and all required placards aboard.

slides.heading: Drugs and alcohol

items: Join a DOT drug testing program, usually through a consortium
Tests: pre-employment, random, post-casualty, reasonable cause
Commercial operators are intoxicated at 0.04% BAC
After a serious marine incident: alcohol test within 2 hours, drugs within 32 hours
Refusing a test can cost you your license

slides.script: As a licensed captain operating commercially, you must take part in a Department of Transportation drug testing program. Most owner-operators join a consortium that handles random testing. Tests are required before employment, at random, after a serious marine incident, and when there’s reasonable cause. For alcohol, a commercial vessel operator is considered intoxicated at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero four percent, half the recreational limit. After a serious marine incident, alcohol testing must be done within two hours and drug testing within thirty-two hours. Refusing a test can cost you your license.

After a serious marine incident, alcohol testing must be done within two hours and drug testing within thirty-two hours. Refusing a test can cost you your license.

slides.heading: Life jackets

items: An approved wearable life jacket for every person aboard
Passenger-carrying vessels: offshore (Type I or equivalent) life jackets
Child sizes for every child
Readily accessible and in good condition
Plus a throwable device, usually a ring buoy

slides.script: Life jackets come first. Every person aboard needs a Coast Guard approved wearable life jacket of the right size, and uninspected passenger vessels carrying passengers for hire must carry the offshore type, traditionally called Type one, with the most flotation. Carry child sizes for every child. Life jackets must be readily accessible, not locked away or still in their plastic, and in serviceable condition, with no rips, rot or missing straps. Newer life jackets use a labeling system with performance levels and icons, but older Type-labeled jackets remain legal while serviceable. You also need a throwable device, usually a ring buoy, ready at hand. Check the regulations for your route on lights and reflective tape.
slides.spoken: Life jackets come first. Every person aboard needs a Coast Guard approved wearable life jacket of the right size, and uninspected passenger vessels carrying passengers for hire must carry the offshore type, traditionally called Type one, with the most flotation. Carry child sizes for every child. Life jackets must be readily accessible, not locked away or still in their plastic, and in serviceable condition, with no rips, rot or missing straps. Newer life jackets use a labeling system with performance levels and icons, but older Type-labeled jackets remain legal while serviceable. You also need a throwable device, usually a ring buoy, ready at hand. Check the regulations for your route on lights and reflective tape.

slides.heading: Fire extinguishers
slides.script: Required portable fire extinguishers depend on boat length. Under twenty-six feet, you need one B-one extinguisher. From twenty-six to under forty feet, two B-ones or one B-two. From forty to sixty-five feet, three B-ones, or one B-two plus one B-one. An approved fixed system in the engine room reduces the requirement by one B-one. Newer extinguishers are labeled five-B and twenty-B instead of B-one and B-two, and boats built in recent years must carry those. Disposable extinguishers must be replaced twelve years after their date of manufacture. Mount them where you can reach them quickly, and check the gauges.

slides.heading: Visual distress signals
slides.script: Visual distress signals are required on coastal waters, which include the ocean, the Gulf, and connected bays and sounds until they narrow to less than two miles wide. Boats sixteen feet and longer must carry signals for both day and night. You can meet that with three pyrotechnic signals good for day and night, such as red hand flares, or with combinations like an orange distress flag for day and an electric distress light for night. Pyrotechnic signals expire forty-two months after manufacture, so check the dates. Never fire flares except in a real emergency.

slides.heading: Ventilation and flame arrestors

items: Gasoline engine spaces need natural and powered ventilation
Run the blower at least 4 minutes before starting
Gasoline inboards need a backfire flame arrestor
Keep arrestors clean and secured
Diesels need ventilation for combustion air

slides.script: Boats with gasoline engines in enclosed spaces must have ventilation to remove explosive vapor, usually natural vents plus a powered blower. Run the blower for at least four minutes before starting the engine, and sniff the bilge. Gasoline inboard and sterndrive engines must have a Coast Guard approved backfire flame arrestor on the carburetor or throttle body, kept clean and firmly secured, so a backfire can’t ignite vapor in the compartment. Diesel engines are far less explosive, but their spaces still need ventilation to supply combustion air.

slides.heading: Everything else aboard

items: Navigation lights and sound-signaling equipment
Oil and garbage placards on boats 26 ft and over
An approved marine sanitation device if there’s a toilet
A pre-departure safety briefing for passengers
Wise extras: EPIRB or PLB, VHF-DSC, first aid kit, high-water alarm

slides.script: Other required equipment includes navigation lights and sound-signaling equipment that meet the Navigation Rules, the oil discharge and garbage placards on boats twenty-six feet and over, and a Coast Guard certified marine sanitation device if you have an installed toilet. Before every trip, brief your passengers on where the life jackets are, how to put them on, and what to do in an emergency. Beyond the minimum, a professional captain carries a registered EPIRB or personal locator beacon, a VHF radio with DSC, a well-stocked first aid kit, and reliable bilge pumps with a high-water alarm.

slides.heading: How fire works
slides.script: Fire is the emergency every captain dreads, so start with how it works. A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, plus the chemical chain reaction that keeps it going. Remove any one and the fire goes out. Cooling removes heat, smothering removes oxygen, shutting off the fuel removes fuel, and dry chemical agents interrupt the chain reaction. Fires are classed by what’s burning. Class A is ordinary combustibles like wood, cushions and line. Class B is flammable liquids like gasoline and oil, the most common boat fire. Class C is energized electrical equipment. Class D is combustible metals.

slides.heading: Extinguishing agents

head: Agent
Fire classes
Notes
rows: Most common on boats; messy and corrosive
Displaces oxygen; no residue; short range
Never a solid stream on fuel or electrical fires

slides.script: Each extinguishing agent suits certain fires. Dry chemical, rated A B C or B C, is the most common on boats and works on most fires, but it leaves a corrosive powder. Carbon dioxide works on fuel and electrical fires by displacing oxygen, leaves no residue, but has short range and can suffocate people in a closed space. Clean agents are often used in fixed engine-room systems. Foam smothers fuel fires. Water is excellent for Class A fires, but a solid stream on burning fuel spreads it, and on electrical equipment it conducts electricity.

slides.heading: Fighting a fire

items: Raise the alarm; life jackets on; passengers away from the fire
Position the boat so wind carries smoke and flames away
PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep
Keep an escape route behind you
Not out in seconds? Call Mayday and prepare to abandon

slides.script: When fire breaks out, raise the alarm, get life jackets on everyone, and move passengers away from the fire. Maneuver the boat so the wind carries smoke and flames away from people, which often means putting the fire downwind. Use a portable extinguisher with PASS: pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle and sweep side to side. Keep an escape route behind you. Small boat fires grow very fast, so if the fire isn’t out within seconds, call Mayday and prepare to abandon the boat.

slides.heading: Engine compartment fires

items: Shut down engines, generator, blowers and fuel
Close vents and hatches to starve the fire
Don’t open the hatch: fresh air feeds it
Discharge the fixed system if it hasn’t fired
Wait at least 15 minutes before opening; extinguisher ready

slides.script: Engine compartment fires are the most dangerous on small boats. Shut down the engines, generator and blowers, and close the fuel valves. Close vents and hatches to starve the fire of oxygen, and don’t open the engine hatch, since a rush of fresh air can make it flare violently. Discharge the fixed extinguishing system if it hasn’t fired automatically. Many systems shut down the engines when they discharge. Then wait at least fifteen minutes for the compartment to cool before opening it, so the fire doesn’t reignite, and have a portable extinguisher ready when you do.

slides.heading: Electrical, galley and propane fires

items: Electrical: kill the power, then CO2 or dry chemical
Galley grease: smother with a lid or fire blanket, never water
Propane: close the tank valve; vapor sinks into the bilge
Fire blanket for clothing and small galley fires

slides.script: For an electrical fire, kill the power at the battery switch or breaker first, then use carbon dioxide or dry chemical. For a grease fire on a galley stove, smother it with a lid or a fire blanket and turn off the heat. Never use water, which makes burning grease explode outward. Propane is heavier than air, so a leak sinks into the bilge just like gasoline vapor. Close the valve at the tank, and if you smell propane, ventilate thoroughly before any spark. A fire blanket is also the fastest way to smother burning clothing.

lessons.title: Fueling, fire prevention and carbon monoxide

slides.heading: Gasoline vapor

items: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and settles in the bilge
A small amount of vapor can cause a powerful explosion
Propane behaves the same way
Diesel is far less volatile, but still burns

slides.script: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air, so it flows downhill and collects in the bilge and low compartments, where a single spark from a switch, pump or starter can ignite it. A surprisingly small amount of vaporized gasoline can produce an explosion strong enough to destroy a boat. Propane behaves the same way. Diesel fuel is much less volatile and much harder to ignite, which is one reason most commercial boats run diesel, but it still burns once lit. Most boat explosions happen during or just after fueling.

slides.heading: Safe fueling, step by step

lines: Moor securely; passengers ashore if practical
Stop engines and motors; no smoking or open flame
Close hatches, ports and cabin doors
Keep the nozzle touching the fill pipe; don’t overfill
Wipe up spills, open up, run the blower 4+ minutes and sniff the bilge

slides.script: Fuel with a routine every time. Moor securely and, if practical, have passengers wait ashore. Stop the engines and all electrical motors, and allow no smoking or open flame. Close hatches, ports and cabin doors so vapor can’t get below. Keep the nozzle in contact with the fill pipe to prevent a static spark, and don’t overfill, since fuel expands as it warms. Afterward, wipe up any spills, open everything, run the blower for at least four minutes, and sniff the bilge and engine compartment before starting the engine.

Close hatches, ports and cabin doors so vapor can’t get below. Keep the nozzle in contact with the fill pipe to prevent a static spark, and don’t overfill, since fuel expands as it warms. Afterward, wipe up any spills, open everything, run the blower for at least four minutes, and sniff the bilge and engine compartment before starting the engine.

slides.heading: Carbon monoxide

items: Colorless, odorless and deadly
Builds near the stern, the swim platform and enclosed cabins
“Station wagon effect”: exhaust drawn aboard while underway
Symptoms mimic seasickness: headache, nausea, dizziness
Install CO alarms; no one on the swim platform with engines or generator running

slides.script: Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas in engine and generator exhaust, and it kills boaters every year. It builds up near the stern, on and around the swim platform, and in enclosed cabins. Underway, the station wagon effect can draw exhaust back aboard, especially with a canvas enclosure. Early symptoms, like headache, nausea and dizziness, are easily mistaken for seasickness. Install and test carbon monoxide alarms in enclosed spaces, never let anyone hang on the swim platform or teak-surf with an engine or generator running, and move anyone with symptoms into fresh air and get medical help.

slides.heading: Batteries and electrical systems

items: Charging batteries give off explosive hydrogen
Ventilate and secure batteries; cover the terminals
Use marine-rated wiring, breakers and fuses
Shore power: inspect cords and connectors
Electric shock drowning: never swim near docks with shore power

slides.script: Batteries give off explosive hydrogen gas while charging, so battery compartments need ventilation, and batteries must be secured so they can’t shift in a seaway, with terminals covered. Use marine-rated wiring, breakers and fuses, since many boat fires start with electrical faults. Inspect shore power cords and connectors for heat damage. And remember electric shock drowning. Faulty wiring can energize the water around docks, especially in fresh or brackish water, so never let anyone swim near a marina or dock with shore power.

slides.heading: Good housekeeping

items: Keep bilges clean and free of oil and fuel
Inspect fuel lines, clamps, vents and tanks regularly
Store rags, paints and solvents properly
Smoking only where it’s safe, if at all
Prevention is far easier than firefighting

slides.script: Most boat fires are preventable. Keep bilges clean and free of oil and fuel, which also helps you spot new leaks. Inspect fuel lines, hose clamps, tank vents and fuel tanks regularly for chafe, corrosion and seepage. Store oily rags, paints and solvents in proper containers, since oily rags can heat up and ignite on their own. Limit smoking to safe areas, if you allow it at all. A few minutes of inspection before each trip is far easier than fighting a fire offshore with six passengers aboard.

slides.heading: G, B and M
slides.script: Stability is about where the weight is. G is the center of gravity, which pulls down. B is the center of buoyancy, the center of the underwater hull, which pushes up. When the boat heels, B moves toward the low side, and the two forces create a righting arm, labeled G Z, that pushes the boat back upright. M, the metacenter, is where the vertical line through B crosses the centerline. The distance from G up to M is called the metacentric height, G M. A bigger G M means more initial stability.

M, the metacenter, is where the vertical line through B crosses the centerline. The distance from G up to M is called the metacentric height, G M. A bigger G M means more initial stability.

slides.heading: What hurts stability

items: Weight added high raises G
Free surface: sloshing liquid acts like raising G
Keep tanks full or empty, and bilges dry
Quick, snappy roll: stiff, large GM
Slow, lazy roll: tender, small GM

slides.script: Anything that raises G reduces stability: passengers crowding a tower, gear stacked high, a heavy load on the cabin top. Free surface effect is just as dangerous. Liquid sloshing in a half-full tank, or water in the bilge or on deck, shifts to the low side and acts like raising G. Keep tanks full or empty, and keep bilges dry. You can feel stability in the roll. A quick, snappy roll means a stiff boat with a large G M. A slow, lazy roll means a tender boat with a small G M, and that’s a warning sign.

slides.heading: Passengers and loading

items: Passengers rushing to one rail can capsize a small boat
Keep heavy loads low and centered
Respect the capacity plate on small boats
Fuel, ice and fish change your loading during the day
Water on deck acts like free surface

slides.script: On a charter, your biggest stability variable is people. When someone hooks a big fish, everyone wants to rush to one rail, and on a small boat that can be enough to capsize or swamp it. Keep passengers spread out and seated when running, and keep heavy loads like coolers and ice low and centered. Respect the capacity plate on small boats. Remember that loading changes during the day: you burn fuel, melt ice, and fill the fish box. And water trapped on deck acts just like free surface.

slides.heading: Words to know

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Temporary lean from wind, waves or a turn
Steady lean from off-center weight or flooding
Fore-and-aft balance: down by the bow or stern
Height from the waterline to the deck edge

slides.script: A few terms. Heel is a temporary lean caused by wind, waves or a turn. List is a steady lean caused by off-center weight or by flooding, and an unexplained list is a warning that water may be getting in. Trim is the fore-and-aft balance, described as down by the bow or down by the stern. Freeboard is the height from the waterline to the deck edge, and reserve buoyancy is the watertight volume above the waterline that keeps you afloat as you take on water or load.
